one: Vertical: a bigger machine. Horizontal: more machines sharing the work.
an: Vertical is buying a bigger truck. Horizontal is buying more trucks, which also means you now need dispatchers and routes.
how: Vertical: more CPU/RAM. No code changes, has a ceiling and a single point of failure, often needs a restart.
Horizontal: add instances behind a load balancer. Near-unlimited for stateless tiers, gives redundancy, requires the app to be stateless.
Databases are the hard part: reads scale with replicas and caches; writes need partitioning or sharding.
why: The first move in almost every system-design answer: what scales how, and where is the bottleneck?
trade: Vertical scaling is underrated. Modern machines are huge, and "just use a bigger DB instance" buys years for many products.

myth.r: Horizontal for stateless app servers, yes. For databases, scaling up first is often the smartest, cheapest move.

q.s: App servers are at 20% CPU; the single Postgres instance is at 95%. What does adding more app servers do?
o: Fixes it
Nothing good, and likely worse (more connections to an overloaded DB)
Halves DB load
Shards automatically
q.e: Scale the bottleneck: optimise queries, add indexes, cache, add read replicas, or scale the DB up.

more: Finding the bottleneck with load tests (k6, autocannon)
Read/write ratio as a design input
Vertical limits of managed DB tiers
Cost per request as a scaling metric
lab: Load test a local API with k6 at increasing rates until latency degrades. Watch CPU of the app and of Postgres to see which saturates first.
Run two app instances behind nginx and repeat; note whether throughput doubled.

plain:
When your system needs to handle more work, you have two options. Vertical: move to a bigger machine (more CPU, more memory). Horizontal: add more machines and split the work between them.

Vertical is simple but has a ceiling. Horizontal can grow much further but requires your app to work correctly with several copies running at once.
bridge: Upgrading your Supabase or database plan to a larger instance is vertical scaling. Netlify running your function on many instances at once is horizontal scaling.

walk.title: Finding what to scale
steps: Traffic doubles and the app slows down.
Monitoring: app servers at 25% CPU, database at 95% CPU.
Adding app servers (horizontal) would not help; it would send even more queries to the busy database.
First fix the expensive queries (indexes, N+1). Database CPU drops to 50%.
Then decide: a bigger database instance (vertical) buys years; read replicas or caching come next if needed.

terms: The part that limits the whole system.
Holding no user data in memory, so any copy can serve any request.
insights: Before scaling out, multiply: replicas × pool size, replicas × partner API calls. Scale-out moves the bottleneck downstream.
A bigger instance buys time cheaply. Use that time to fix the queries that made it necessary.
Replicas across zones are an availability decision. Keep 2–3 even when one machine could carry the load.

prod.summary: In production, scaling starts with finding the bottleneck under realistic load, then scaling that part. Stateless app servers scale out easily; databases usually scale up first, then with read replicas, caching and connection pooling, and only then with sharding. Seniors check that every layer can follow: connection limits, autoscaling signals and third-party quotas.
checklist: Load tests (k6, Locust) run before launches at 2–3× expected peak, and the team knows which resource saturates first.
The autoscaling signal matches the workload: CPU for CPU-bound services, queue age or backlog for workers, concurrency or RPS per pod for I/O-bound APIs.
Connection math holds at max replicas: pods × pool size stays under the database limit, or a pooler such as PgBouncer sits in between.
Database headroom is tracked (CPU, IOPS, storage growth, replica lag), with the next step already chosen: bigger instance, replica or cache.
Scale-in is safe: pods handle SIGTERM and drain in-flight requests within the grace period.
At least 2–3 replicas across zones, for availability, not only for load.
numbers: PostgreSQL default max_connections is 100, and every connection is a backend process with its own memory.
Kubernetes HPA: no scaling while the metric is within 10% of the target (tolerance 0.1); scale-down uses a 300 s stabilization window by default; the controller checks every 15 s.
Kubernetes gives a pod 30 s by default (terminationGracePeriodSeconds) between SIGTERM and SIGKILL.
Little's law: in-flight requests = throughput × latency. 1,000 req/s × 0.1 s = 100 in flight, so if latency doubles you need twice the concurrency at the same traffic.
failures: The autoscaler adds pods, latency gets worse, and the database logs too many clients already.
The bottleneck is the database, and more pods meant more connections. Cap max replicas by database capacity, add PgBouncer, and fix slow queries first.
The HPA targets 70% CPU and never scales, yet p99 latency is 3 s.
The service is I/O-bound (waiting on the database or APIs), so CPU stays low. Scale on concurrency, requests per pod or queue length instead.
Every scale-in causes a burst of 502 errors.
Pods exit right away on SIGTERM while the load balancer still sends them traffic. Fail readiness, wait a few seconds (preStop), drain, then exit.
A 4× larger database instance gave only 1.3× more throughput.
The limit was lock contention or one hot row, not CPU. Check wait events (pg_stat_activity.wait_event) and lock waits before buying hardware.

code.title: HPA with limits that respect the database
code.note: maxReplicas is a database decision, not only a cost decision. CPU utilisation is measured against the pod's CPU request, so requests must be set.
code.src:
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: api
  minReplicas: 3      # spread over 3 zones: availability, not load
  maxReplicas: 20     # 20 pods x pool of 4 = 80 DB connections (< max_connections 100)
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 65   # % of the CPU *request*: requests must be set
  behavior:
    scaleUp:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0
      policies:
        - type: Percent
          value: 100               # at most double every 60 s
          periodSeconds: 60
    scaleDown:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300   # the default: avoids flapping

qs.s: Worker pods consume a queue; most of each job is waiting on an external API. Which autoscaling signal fits best?
o: CPU utilisation
Memory usage
Queue backlog per worker or age of the oldest message (for example with KEDA)
Number of nodes in the cluster
qs.e: I/O-bound workers can be overloaded at 10% CPU. Backlog and message age measure the thing users feel: how long work waits.

qs.s: A read-heavy app (95% reads) has Postgres at 85% CPU after slow queries were fixed. Writes are light. Cheapest effective next step?
o: Cache hot reads and/or add a read replica, sending reads that tolerate a little lag to it
Shard the database by user ID
Add more app pods
Split the app into microservices
qs.e: With mostly reads, replicas and caches remove load without changing the data model. Sharding is for when writes or data size outgrow one primary. More app pods only add database load.

qs.s: An API pod handles 50 concurrent requests well. Traffic is 400 req/s with 250 ms average latency. How many pods do you need?
o: At least 2 (400 × 0.25 = 100 concurrent ÷ 50 per pod); run 3 or more for headroom and zone failures
qs.e: Little's law turns rate and latency into concurrency: 100 requests are in flight on average. Divide by per-pod capacity, then add headroom for spikes and losing a zone.

qs.s: Read the autoscaler status. CPU requests are set correctly. What does the HPA do next, and what should you check?

code.title: kubectl get hpa
code.src:
$ kubectl get hpa api
NAME   REFERENCE        TARGETS         MINPODS   MAXPODS   REPLICAS
api    Deployment/api   cpu: 140%/70%   3         10        6

o: It adds one pod per minute until CPU is under 70%
Nothing: the 10% tolerance means it waits until CPU is 154%

It wants ceil(6 × 140 / 70) = 12 pods but stops at the max of 10. If 10 pods are not enough, CPU and latency stay high, so check whether the real bottleneck (often the database) can take more pods before raising maxReplicas
It scales to 12, because maxReplicas is only a soft limit
qs.e: The HPA formula is desired = ceil(current × current metric / target). The result is always clamped to maxReplicas. The tempting “raise the max” is only right if the database and other shared limits can handle more pods.

qs.s: Each pod creates this pool. The HPA allows up to 15 pods. Postgres runs with max_connections = 200. What happens at peak traffic?

code.title: db.ts

o: At 15 pods the pools can open 15 × 20 = 300 connections, more than 200 (and a few are reserved for superusers). New connections fail with too many clients already, exactly when traffic is highest
Nothing: pg shares one pool across all pods
Postgres queues the extra connections until others close
Only idle connections are counted, so it is safe
qs.e: Connection math must hold at maxReplicas, not at the normal replica count. Fix it with smaller pools, a lower max replica count, or a pooler such as PgBouncer in transaction mode. Postgres does not queue connections; it rejects them. For a role without SUPERUSER, the first error is often “remaining connection slots are reserved for roles with the SUPERUSER attribute”: the same limit, reached a few connections earlier.

qs.s: A write-heavy Postgres on 16 vCPU runs at 70% CPU at peak, and load grows about 5% per month. Queries are already tuned. What is the most sensible plan?
o: Shard by customer now, before it is too late
Add three read replicas
Add more app pods
Move to a larger instance (for example 32 vCPU) to buy time, and in parallel reduce write volume (archiving, batching) and plan partitioning for when even the largest instance is not enough
qs.e: At 5% growth per month you have roughly a year before 100%. Scaling up is fast and needs no code changes. Read replicas do not help writes, and sharding is a large, slow project that should start only when the numbers show you need it.

qs.s: In a load test, throughput stops at 2,000 req/s. App CPU is 40%, database CPU is 30%, and p99 latency climbs fast. The pool metric waitingCount is high. What is the bottleneck?
o: CPU on the app pods
The database connection pool: requests wait for a free connection, so latency grows while CPU stays low. Check pool size against Little's law and the database limit
Network bandwidth
Garbage collection in Node.js
qs.e: When every resource looks idle but latency rises, look for a queue: a pool, a semaphore, a lock. Little's law tells you how many connections you need: 2,000 req/s × 10 ms of DB time = 20 in flight per pod group.

interview.q: Our API latency doubled after traffic grew three times. Walk me through how you would find what to scale.
answer: Start from user-facing metrics (p50/p99 latency, error rate) and break down where time goes with tracing: app code, database, external calls.
Check saturation of each resource: CPU, memory, connection pools, DB CPU and IOPS, lock waits, queue age. The resource that is full (or has a queue in front of it) is the bottleneck.
Fix cheap things first: slow queries, missing indexes, N+1 calls, caching hot reads.
Scale the bottleneck itself: more app pods only if the app is the limit; bigger DB, replicas or a cache if the database is the limit.
Re-run a load test at 2–3× expected peak to confirm, and check that limits still hold at max replicas (DB connections, third-party quotas).
followups: How would you tell an I/O-bound service from a CPU-bound one?
What signal would you autoscale on for a queue worker?

interview.q: When would you scale a database vertically instead of horizontally, and where does that stop working?
answer: Vertical first in most products: no code change, no distributed transactions, and cloud instances go up to hundreds of vCPUs and terabytes of RAM.
Reads scale out cheaply with replicas and caches, as long as the app tolerates replica lag.
Vertical stops working when writes or data size outgrow the largest instance, when failover or restart times on a huge instance are too long, or when cost per step becomes very high.
Lock contention or one hot row does not improve with more hardware; check wait events before buying.
Horizontal write scaling (sharding or a distributed SQL database) brings cross-shard queries, rebalancing and operational cost, so it needs a clear numbers-based reason.
followups: How do you pick a shard key?
What breaks when you add a read replica?

interview.q: System design: a web app has 1,000 concurrent users today. How does the architecture change as it grows to 100,000 and then 1 million?
answer: 1k: one app server and one database, with backups and monitoring. Do not over-build.
10k–100k: stateless app servers behind a load balancer, a CDN for static assets, a cache (Redis) for hot reads, connection pooling, a read replica, background jobs on a queue.
1M: multiple zones, autoscaling on the right signal, async processing for heavy work, careful database scaling (bigger instance, more replicas, then partitioning or sharding for write-heavy tables).
At each step, use estimation: requests per second at peak, data growth, connections, and cost per request.
Name the bottleneck at each stage instead of adding components because big companies use them.
followups: Where would you put the cache, and how would you invalidate it?
At what point would you shard, and how?

videos.t: System Design BASICS: Horizontal vs. Vertical Scaling
videos.why: Horizontal vs vertical scaling, the classic explanation.

one: A server that keeps no user-specific data in its own memory or disk between requests. Any instance can handle any request.
an: A call centre where every agent reads the shared customer file, not one where only "your" agent remembers your case.
how: State lives in shared systems: database, Redis, object storage, the client (signed cookies/tokens).
Then instances are interchangeable: kill, add, restart, deploy, autoscale freely.
Things that quietly break statelessness: in-memory sessions, local file uploads, in-process caches assumed to be authoritative, cron jobs running on every instance.
why: Horizontal scaling, rolling deploys, autoscaling and container platforms all assume it.
trade: Every state lookup is now a network call. In-process caches are fine as long as they are treated as disposable copies.

myth.m: Stateless means the app has no state.
myth.r: The system has plenty of state; it just does not live in the app process.

q.s: After scaling to 3 instances, a nightly email cron sends every email 3 times. Why?
o: Email provider bug
Each instance runs the scheduler; scheduled jobs need a single runner or a distributed lock
DNS
CORS
q.e: Use a dedicated scheduler, a job queue with unique jobs, or a lock (e.g. Postgres advisory lock).

more: Sticky sessions and when they are acceptable
lab: Audit one of your backends for hidden state: in-memory maps, local file writes, timers, schedulers. Move each to Redis, object storage, or a job queue.
Implement a Postgres advisory lock so a cron job runs on only one of several instances.

plain:
A stateless server keeps nothing about users in its own memory or disk between requests. Sessions, uploads, caches and jobs live in shared places: the database, Redis, object storage.

Then every copy of the server is identical and replaceable. You can add, remove or restart any of them at any time.
bridge: Serverless functions force this on you: each call may run on a different instance, so you cannot keep anything in a global variable. Container-based backends should follow the same rule voluntarily.

walk.title: Hidden state that breaks when you add a second server
steps: Sessions stored in an in-memory object → users get logged out when their next request hits the other server.
Uploaded files saved to ./uploads → the file exists on server A only; server B returns 404.
A setInterval that sends daily emails → runs on both servers; every email goes out twice.
An in-memory rate limit counter → each server counts separately; the real limit is doubled.
Fix each: sessions → Redis/DB, files → object storage, scheduled jobs → one scheduler or a lock, counters → Redis.

terms: No per-user data kept inside the server process.
Data in a system all servers use, like Redis or the DB.
Container storage that disappears on restart.
A lock shared across servers so only one does a task.
insights: Test it the hard way: run 2+ replicas with round-robin and kill one in the middle of the test.
Sticky sessions hide state; they do not remove it. A deploy or scale-in still loses it.
Graceful shutdown is part of being stateless: a pod that dies mid-request loses that work even if it stores nothing.

prod.summary: In production, “stateless” is checked, not assumed: anything in process memory or on local disk must be safe to lose at any moment, because deploys, autoscaling and node failures kill pods. Seniors look for hidden state (sessions, uploads, timers, in-memory rate limits, WebSocket rooms), move it to shared stores, and make shutdown graceful.
checklist: Sessions live in a shared store or in a signed or encrypted cookie; no in-memory session store in production.
Uploads go straight to object storage (pre-signed URLs), not to the container's disk.
Scheduled jobs run once: a separate scheduler, a queue with unique jobs, or a lock such as pg_try_advisory_lock.
Rate limits, counters and idempotency records are in Redis or the database, not in per-process maps.
Real-time features (WebSockets, SSE) fan out through shared pub/sub (Redis, NATS), so messages reach users connected to other pods.
SIGTERM is handled: fail readiness, stop accepting, finish in-flight requests, close pools, exit within the grace period.
Tested with 2+ replicas behind round-robin, killing one replica in the middle of the test.
numbers: Kubernetes terminationGracePeriodSeconds defaults to 30 s; after that the container is killed with SIGKILL.

Node.js server.keepAliveTimeout is 5 s in Node.js 22, 24 and 26; the change to 65 s is on Node's main branch for the next major release (27), not in any release yet. An AWS ALB keeps idle connections for 60 s by default. If Node closes an idle connection first, the ALB can return sporadic 502s, so set it above the ALB's value (and headersTimeout a little higher).
AWS ALB sticky-session cookies last 1 day by default, so “sticky sessions” hide in-memory state for a day, not forever.
failures: Users are logged out at random after scaling to 3 pods.
An in-memory session store (for example the default express-session MemoryStore). Move sessions to Redis or the database, or use signed stateless tokens.
Uploaded avatars return 404 about half of the time.
Files are written to one pod's local disk; other pods do not have them, and they disappear on restart. Upload to object storage and save the object key.
Every deploy causes a burst of 502 and connection-reset errors.
Pods exit immediately on SIGTERM. Fail readiness, wait a few seconds for the load balancer to update, finish in-flight requests, then exit.
Chat messages reach only some members of a room.
Room membership is stored in each pod's memory, and members are on different pods. Fan out through Redis pub/sub or a managed real-time service.

code.title: Graceful shutdown, ALB-safe keep-alive, and a single-run scheduled job
code.note: The advisory lock prevents two runs at the same time, not a second run later. Record that the job is done for the date if “exactly once per day” matters.

qs.s: Which of these is fine to keep in process memory on a stateless API?
o: The list of users currently in a chat room
A copy of the country list, loaded at startup and refreshed every 10 minutes
Shopping carts of logged-in users
A counter used to stop free-trial signups at 1,000
qs.e: A disposable cache of shared, read-only data is fine: losing it costs only a reload. The others are user or global state that must be shared by all replicas and survive restarts.

qs.s: A daily job uses pg_try_advisory_lock and finishes in 2 s. Timers on replicas can fire up to 10 s apart. What can still go wrong?
o: Nothing: advisory locks make it run exactly once
Postgres deadlocks
The lock is never released
A replica whose timer fires 10 s later finds the lock free and runs the job again; also record completion (a job_runs row per date) or use one scheduler
qs.e: A lock only stops overlap. Once the first run finishes and unlocks, a late replica can take it. Idempotency (“done for 2026-10-03”) or a single scheduler makes it once per day.

qs.s: On SIGTERM during a deploy, your pod calls process.exit() immediately. What do users see?
o: Some in-flight requests fail, and for a few seconds new requests still reach the closed pod (502 or connection reset)
Nothing: Kubernetes moves the requests to another pod
Only WebSocket users notice anything
The deploy is rolled back automatically
qs.e: Endpoint removal and SIGTERM happen in parallel, so traffic keeps arriving for a short time. Fail readiness, wait a few seconds, drain, then exit.

qs.s: This logout code runs on 4 API replicas behind round-robin. What happens after a user logs out?

code.title: auth.ts

o: Logout works everywhere, because the Set is shared by Node.js

The token is still accepted by the other 3 replicas, and by all 4 after the next restart. Store revoked IDs in Redis with a TTL equal to the token's remaining lifetime, or use short-lived tokens with refresh
JWTs cannot be revoked in any way, so the code does nothing
It only fails when sticky sessions are turned on
qs.e: Each process has its own memory, so the Set is per replica and disappears on restart. A shared store fixes both problems. JWTs can be revoked, but only with shared state or short lifetimes.

qs.s: A chat feature uses Socket.IO on 6 pods. Users in the same room only see some of the messages. Sticky sessions are already on. Which change fixes it?

code.title: chat.ts

o: Make sticky sessions last longer
Run one bigger pod instead of 6
Increase the ping interval
Add a shared adapter (for example @socket.io/redis-adapter) so io.to(room).emit is published to every pod and each pod delivers to its own sockets
qs.e: Sticky sessions keep one user on one pod, but members of a room are on different pods. The room's membership is state that must be shared, so broadcasts go through pub/sub. One big pod “works” but removes redundancy and has a ceiling.

qs.s: Each pod caches user permissions in memory for 10 minutes. An admin removes a user's access to a project. What is the risk?
o: For up to 10 minutes, and differently on each pod, the user can still use the removed access. For security data use a short TTL, invalidate through pub/sub, or read permissions from the shared store
No risk: in-memory caches are always disposable
The cache is cleared automatically when the database changes
Only the pod that handled the admin request is affected
qs.e: Local caches are fine as copies, but a copy can be stale. For catalog data a few minutes of staleness is fine. For permissions, it is a security gap, so the staleness budget must be very short or the cache must be invalidated.

qs.s: An app keeps sessions in memory and uses ALB sticky sessions so each user stays on one pod. What happens during a scale-in from 6 to 4 pods?
o: Nothing: the ALB moves the sessions to the remaining pods
Kubernetes copies the memory of removed pods to new ones
Users on the 2 removed pods lose their sessions and are logged out (or lose carts); the same happens on every deploy and crash
Only users who were idle are affected
qs.e: Stickiness only routes requests; it does not move state. Any event that kills a pod (deploy, scale-in, node failure) loses its memory. That is why sessions belong in a shared store or a signed cookie.

interview.q: What does it mean for a service to be stateless, and where does the state go?
answer: The process keeps nothing between requests that another instance would need: no sessions, uploads, counters or scheduled jobs that only it knows about.
State moves to systems built for it: the database, Redis, object storage, a queue, or the client (signed or encrypted cookies, tokens).
Disposable copies are still allowed: an in-process cache of shared data that can be lost and reloaded.
This makes instances interchangeable, which is what autoscaling, rolling deploys and crash recovery need.
The cost is a network call for every state lookup, and a shared store that must itself be scaled and made highly available.
followups: Is a WebSocket server stateless?
How do you make a scheduled job run only once across replicas?

interview.q: How do you shut down a stateless service without dropping requests during a deploy?
answer: Handle SIGTERM: fail the readiness probe so the load balancer stops sending new traffic.
Wait a few seconds, because endpoint removal and SIGTERM happen in parallel and traffic keeps arriving briefly (a preStop sleep does the same).
Stop accepting new connections, finish in-flight requests, close idle keep-alive connections, then close database pools and exit.
All of this must fit in terminationGracePeriodSeconds (30 s by default) or the process is killed with SIGKILL.
Long work (exports, emails) should not run inside a web request at all; put it on a queue so a killed pod does not lose it.
followups: Why can a too-short keep-alive timeout cause 502s behind a load balancer?
How do you drain long-lived WebSocket connections?

interview.q: System design: design the session and authentication layer for a web app that runs on 20 replicas.
answer: Option 1: server-side sessions in Redis or the database, referenced by an opaque, HttpOnly, Secure cookie. Easy to revoke; one store lookup per request.
Option 2: signed tokens (JWT) with short lifetimes (minutes) plus refresh tokens stored server-side. No lookup per request, but revocation needs a denylist or waiting for expiry.
Whatever you choose, nothing lives in one replica's memory; the session store needs replication and a failure plan.
Rate limits, login attempt counters and CSRF tokens also go into the shared store.
Trade-off to state clearly: lookups and a dependency on the store versus delayed revocation.
followups: How do you log a user out of all devices?
What happens if Redis is down?

videos.t: Stateful vs Stateless Architecture - System Design Basics
videos.why: Stateful vs stateless architecture and why it matters for scaling.

one: When a network partition splits a distributed system, it must choose: stay consistent (refuse some requests) or stay available (answer with possibly stale data).
an: Two bank branches lose their phone line. Either both stop accepting withdrawals (consistent), or both keep serving and risk the same money being withdrawn twice (available).
how: C = every read sees the latest write. A = every request gets a non-error response. P = the system keeps working despite lost messages between nodes.
Partitions happen in real networks, so P is not optional. The real choice is C or A during a partition.
PACELC extends it: Else (no partition), you still trade Latency against Consistency. Synchronous replication = consistent but slower.
why: It is the vocabulary for discussing distributed databases and for explaining why "just replicate it" is not free.
trade: Different data in one product can choose differently: payment balances want consistency; like counts and feeds can be eventually consistent.

myth.m: Pick 2 of 3, so I can pick C and A.
myth.r: Without partition tolerance you are not distributed. CA only exists on a single node.

q.s: A shopping cart service must keep accepting "add to cart" during a network split between data centres, and merge later. Which side of CAP?
o: CP
AP, with conflict resolution on merge
CA
None
q.e: Amazon's original Dynamo made exactly this choice for carts: availability first, reconcile later.

plain:
A distributed database runs on several machines. Sometimes the network between them breaks (a “partition”). During that moment, the system must choose: refuse some requests to avoid giving wrong answers (consistency), or keep answering everyone and risk some answers being out of date (availability).

It cannot have both during a partition. That is the CAP theorem.
bridge: Offline-first apps face the same choice: when the phone has no connection, do you block the user's edits (consistent) or accept them and sync later, maybe with conflicts (available)?

walk.title: Two data centres lose contact
steps: Your database runs in Seoul and Tokyo. The link between them goes down.
A user in Seoul updates their account balance. Tokyo cannot hear about it.
Choice C: Tokyo refuses balance reads and writes until the link returns. Correct, but unavailable for Tokyo users.
Choice A: Tokyo keeps answering with its last known balance. Available, but possibly wrong; conflicting writes must be merged later.
Bank balances usually choose C. Shopping carts and like counts usually choose A.

terms: A network failure splitting machines into groups that cannot talk.
Every read sees the latest write.
Every request gets a non-error answer.
Extension: even without partitions, you trade latency for consistency.
insights: For your database, find one answer in the docs: what does a client see when the primary cannot reach its replicas?
Asynchronous replication plus automatic failover means a small, real data-loss window. Know its size (RPO).
Split brain is the CAP failure that hurts most. Fencing the old leader matters more than fast failover.

prod.summary: In production, CAP shows up as configuration, not theory: replication mode, quorum sizes, write concerns and failover rules decide what your database does when a node or a link fails. Seniors ask, per data type, “during a partition, do we prefer an error or a possibly stale or conflicting answer?”, and then check the database is really configured that way.
checklist: For each critical data type (balance, stock, sessions, likes), the team has written down CP or AP behaviour during a partition and who decided it.
The real replication mode is known: PostgreSQL streaming replication is asynchronous unless synchronous_standby_names is set, so a failover can lose the last commits.
In quorum systems, read-after-write data uses R + W > N (for example Cassandra QUORUM writes and reads with replication factor 3).
Automatic failover uses consensus and fencing (for example Patroni with etcd, or a managed database), so an old primary cannot keep accepting writes (split brain).
AP data has a written merge rule (last-writer-wins, version vectors or CRDTs), and the team knows which writes last-writer-wins can silently drop.
It is tested: cut the network between nodes in staging (iptables, tc, Toxiproxy or a chaos tool) and watch what clients see.
numbers: PostgreSQL: synchronous_standby_names is empty by default, so replication is asynchronous; synchronous_commit = on only waits for standbys that are listed there.
MongoDB 5.0+: the default write concern is w: "majority" for most replica sets.
Cassandra with replication factor 3: QUORUM = 2 replicas, so QUORUM writes plus QUORUM reads overlap (2 + 2 > 3).
DynamoDB: an eventually consistent read costs half of a strongly consistent one (0.5 vs 1 read capacity unit per 4 KB).
failures: After an automatic failover, customers report that orders from the last few seconds are gone.
Asynchronous replication: the old primary had commits the replica never received. Use synchronous or quorum commit for that data, or accept and document the data-loss window (RPO).
After a network blip, two nodes both accepted writes; the same username now belongs to two accounts.
Split brain: a new primary was promoted without fencing the old one. Use consensus-based failover that fences the old leader, and unique constraints enforced on a single writer.
During a cross-region link failure, checkout in region B returns 500 for 15 minutes.

The database chose consistency: region B could not reach a quorum. If that is not acceptable, design an AP path for that flow (accept orders locally, reconcile stock later) or move users to the healthy region.
Items reappear in the cart after the user deleted them.
An AP store merged concurrent writes after a partition and an older “add” beat the “delete”. Use versioned tombstones or an observed-remove set (a CRDT) for collections.

code.title: PostgreSQL: choose C or latency per transaction
code.note: With ANY 1 of two standbys, one standby can die without blocking commits. With a single synchronous standby, its failure makes every COMMIT wait: that is choosing C over A.

qs.s: Cassandra keyspace with replication factor 3. Writes and reads both use consistency level ONE. A user changes their email and immediately reloads the profile. What can happen?
o: They always see the new email, because Cassandra is strongly consistent
The write fails, because ONE is not allowed with RF=3
The write is rejected until all 3 replicas confirm
The read can hit a replica that has not received the write yet and show the old email, because 1 + 1 is not greater than 3
qs.e: Overlap needs R + W > N. With ONE/ONE (1 + 1 ≤ 3) the read and write may touch different replicas. QUORUM/QUORUM (2 + 2 > 3) guarantees overlap.

qs.s: Postgres has synchronous_standby_names = 'replica_a' (one synchronous standby). replica_a's disk dies. What happens to writes on the primary?
o: They continue normally; Postgres quietly falls back to asynchronous replication
COMMITs wait for a standby that will not answer, so writes hang: the system chose consistency over availability
The primary shuts down to protect data
Writes are kept in replica_a's memory until the disk is replaced
qs.e: Postgres does not silently downgrade. Use ANY 1 (a, b) with two standbys so one can fail, and have a runbook for removing a dead standby from the list.

qs.s: There is no partition. Your team turns on synchronous replication to a standby in another region, 80 ms round trip away. What changes for normal traffic?
o: Every commit takes at least about one extra round trip (~80 ms): the “else, latency vs consistency” part of PACELC
Nothing; synchronous replication only matters during partitions
Reads become 80 ms slower but writes are unchanged
Throughput doubles because two servers share the work
qs.e: CAP only talks about partitions. PACELC adds that even in normal operation, stronger consistency costs latency. That is why cross-region synchronous replication is usually limited to data that truly needs it.

qs.s: Keyspace with replication factor 3. Two of the three replicas for this key are down. What does this output show?

code.title: cqlsh

o: A Cassandra bug: writes should always succeed
The data is lost and must be restored from backup
The client must retry until it works

For this request Cassandra chose consistency: it needs 2 live replicas and has 1, so it refuses. Writing at ONE would succeed (availability), but a later QUORUM read might not see it until hints or repair copy it
qs.e: Cassandra lets you choose C or A per request through the consistency level. QUORUM with only one live replica cannot be met. Blind retries do not help until replicas come back.

qs.s: MongoDB replica set. The app writes with w: 1. The primary acknowledges the write and crashes 200 ms later, before any secondary copied it. A secondary becomes the new primary. What happens to the write?

code.title: orders.ts

o: It is lost from the live data: when the old primary rejoins, it rolls back writes the new primary never had (MongoDB saves them to rollback files). Use w: "majority" for data you cannot lose
The new primary fetches it from the old primary's disk automatically
The driver retries it on the new primary and nothing is lost
MongoDB blocks the election until the old primary returns
qs.e: w: 1 trades durability for latency. Only majority-acknowledged writes survive a failover. The client already got 201, so the user believes the order exists.

qs.s: One Postgres primary with an asynchronous read replica in another zone. The zones lose contact. Is this setup CP or AP?
o: CP, because Postgres is ACID

It does not fit one label: writes behave like CP (only the primary accepts them), reads from the replica stay available but can be stale, and an asynchronous failover can lose acknowledged writes. Describe behaviour per operation
AP, because a replica exists
CA, because there is only one primary
qs.e: CAP labels describe one operation under a partition, not a product. Interviewers like candidates who say what each operation does: who can write, what reads return, and what is lost on failover.

qs.s: A Dynamo-style store uses N = 5 replicas and writes with W = 3. What is the smallest read quorum R that guarantees every read sees the latest successful write, and how many replica failures can writes survive?
o: R = 1; writes survive 4 failures
R = 2; writes survive 3 failures
R = 3 (3 + 3 > 5); writes still succeed with 2 replicas down
R = 5; writes survive 0 failures
qs.e: Overlap needs R + W > N, so R ≥ 3. Writes need 3 of 5 replicas alive, so they tolerate 2 failures. R = 2 is tempting, but 2 + 3 = 5 is not greater than 5, so a read could miss the write.

interview.q: Explain the CAP theorem, and tell me what people most often get wrong about it.
answer: When a network partition splits replicas, each operation must either refuse or wait (consistency) or answer from possibly stale data (availability).
Partitions happen, so “choose 2 of 3” is misleading: the real choice is C or A during a partition. A single-node database is not a CAP system at all.
C in CAP means linearizability, not the C in ACID.
Products are not simply CP or AP; the behaviour depends on configuration and on the operation (quorum levels, write concern, failover settings).
Most of the time there is no partition, and the everyday trade-off is latency versus consistency (PACELC).
followups: What does linearizable mean?
How does a quorum system decide R and W?

interview.q: System design: design a shopping cart and inventory for a store that runs in two regions. Which parts choose consistency and which choose availability?
answer: Cart: availability first. Accept adds and removes in the local region and merge later (CRDT-style sets or per-item versions), because a refused “add to cart” loses sales.
Inventory reservation and payment: consistency. Use one home region per item or a strongly consistent store, and refuse or queue when it cannot be reached.
Accept a little overselling only if the business agrees, and then handle it with apologies, backorders or refunds.
Order history and product pages: eventually consistent replicas and caches are fine.
Say what users see during a partition for each flow, and how data is reconciled afterwards.
followups: How do you merge two carts edited in different regions?
What happens to checkout if the home region is down?

interview.q: What is PACELC, and how does it change the way you choose and configure a database?
answer: PACELC: if there is a Partition, choose A or C; Else, choose Latency or Consistency.
Synchronous or quorum replication gives stronger consistency but adds at least a round trip per write; across regions that can be 50–150 ms.
Asynchronous replication is fast but can lose recent writes on failover and serves stale reads from replicas.

Many databases let you choose per request or per transaction (Cassandra consistency levels, Postgres synchronous_commit, DynamoDB ConsistentRead), so you can pay for consistency only where it matters.
Write down the decision per data type: balances and stock versus likes and feeds.
followups: Where would you place a synchronous standby, and why?
What is your RPO with asynchronous replication?

diagrams.src:
sequenceDiagram
  participant S as Seoul user
  participant DS as Seoul DB
  participant DT as Tokyo DB
  participant T as Tokyo user
  Note over DS,DT: The link between regions is down
  S->>DS: set balance to 50
  DS-xDT: replicate (lost)

one: The spectrum of guarantees about when a write becomes visible to readers: strong, read-your-writes, monotonic, eventual.
an: Strong: everyone sees the scoreboard update at the same instant. Eventual: some fans hear the score a few seconds late, but everyone gets it.
how: Strong / linearizable: reads always see the latest write. Simple to reason about, costs latency and availability.
Eventual: replicas converge if writes stop. Fast and available; readers may see stale data meanwhile.
Practical middle grounds: read-your-writes (you always see your own changes), monotonic reads (you never see time go backwards), causal consistency.
why: Many UX bugs ("I posted but it disappeared") are consistency choices nobody made deliberately.
trade: Design the UI for eventual consistency where you have it: optimistic updates, "processing" states, conflict messages.

myth.m: Eventual consistency means data may be wrong forever.
myth.r: It converges, usually within milliseconds to seconds. The problem is the window, which the UX must handle.

q.s: Users post a comment and the page reloads without it about 5% of the time. Reads come from a lagging replica. Which guarantee is missing?
o: Linearizability for all users
Read-your-writes for the author
Partition tolerance
Durability
q.e: Others seeing it a second late is fine. The author must see their own write.

lab: Build an optimistic "like" button with TanStack Query: update immediately, roll back on error, refetch on settle. Simulate a 30% failure rate.
Try Yjs (a CRDT library) to sync a text field between two tabs.

plain:
When data is copied to several places, how quickly does a change become visible everywhere? Strong consistency: immediately, for everyone. Eventual consistency: soon (usually milliseconds to seconds), but someone might briefly see the old value.

In between are useful guarantees, like “you always see your own changes immediately”.
bridge: Optimistic UI updates in React Query are a frontend tool for eventual consistency: show the change immediately, confirm it with the server later, and roll back if it failed.

walk.title: The disappearing comment
steps: A user posts a comment. It is written to the primary database.
The page reloads and reads comments from a replica that is 300ms behind. The new comment is not there. The user posts again: now there are two.
Option 1 (UI): insert the comment into the list optimistically; do not depend on the reload.
Option 2 (backend): read-your-writes: this user's reads go to the primary for a few seconds after writing.
Other users seeing the comment 300ms later is fine. The author must see it immediately.

terms: All reads see the latest write.
Copies converge after a short delay.
A user always sees their own changes.
Showing a change before the server confirms it.
insights: Write a staleness budget per read path (“feed 5 s, balance 0 s”), then route reads to match it.
Returning the new state in the write response removes most read-your-writes bugs without any routing tricks.
Never make a decision (stock, coupon, balance) on a replica or cached value.

prod.summary: In production you rarely pick “strong or eventual” for a whole system. You pick it per read path: which reads may go to a lagging replica or a cache, and which must see the latest write. Seniors measure replica lag, send read-after-write paths to the primary, and design the UI for the gap.
checklist: Every read path that uses a replica or cache has a written staleness budget (for example “feed: 5 s, balance: 0 s”).
Read-your-writes is implemented for the author: reads go to the primary for a short window after a write, or the write response returns the new state.
Replica lag is graphed and alerted (PostgreSQL pg_stat_replication.replay_lag on the primary, or now() - pg_last_xact_replay_timestamp() on the replica; Aurora AuroraReplicaLag).
When lag is above budget, the app automatically stops sending sensitive reads to that replica.
Updates use version checks (WHERE version = $n, or ETag with If-Match) so a stale read cannot cause a lost update.
Decisions such as “is there stock?” or “is this coupon used?” are made by an atomic statement on the primary, never on a cached or replica value.
numbers: Amazon S3 has had strong read-after-write consistency for all PUT and DELETE requests since December 2020.
DynamoDB reads are eventually consistent by default; ConsistentRead: true costs twice as much, and global secondary indexes only support eventually consistent reads.

PostgreSQL replica lag is usually milliseconds, but replay can pause for conflicting queries on the standby up to max_standby_streaming_delay (default 30 s), and big batch writes can push lag to minutes.
failures: “I changed my name but the page still shows the old one”, only for a few seconds and only sometimes.
The read after the write hits a lagging replica or a cache. Route the author's reads to the primary for a short window, or return the updated object in the write response and render it.
Stock goes negative in a flash sale even though the code checks stock > 0 first.

The check read from a replica or cache, then the write went to the primary. Make it one atomic statement on the primary: UPDATE items SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = $1 AND stock > 0, and check the affected row count.
A comment appears, disappears on refresh, then appears again.
No monotonic reads: each request hits a different replica with different lag. Pin a session to one replica, or send the last-seen version and only use replicas that have caught up.
Replica lag alert at 4 minutes during the nightly import; dashboards show yesterday's numbers.
One huge transaction, or long queries on the replica, hold back replay. Split the import into smaller transactions and route freshness-sensitive reads to the primary while lag is above budget.

code.title: Read-your-writes: route the author's reads to the primary for a short window
code.note: The window only works if it is longer than real lag. If lag can reach minutes (batch jobs), also check measured lag before using the replica.

qs.s: Two support agents open ticket 77 at version 4. Agent A saves a status change. Ten seconds later agent B, still on the old page, saves a priority change, and the form sends the whole ticket. Without any checks, what happens, and what is the fix?
o: Both changes are kept, because databases merge rows
B's save fails because of eventual consistency
B's save overwrites A's status change (a lost update). Use a version check such as UPDATE … WHERE id = 77 AND version = 4 and ask B to reload when 0 rows change
Give agent B read-your-writes
qs.e: This is a concurrency problem, not replica lag. Optimistic concurrency (a version column or ETag + If-Match) detects that B edited an old copy. Read-your-writes only helps users see their own writes.

qs.s: A read replica is about 3 s behind. Which query is safe to serve from it?
o: A public “trending posts” list
Checking the password right after the user changed it
“Has this one-time coupon already been used?” before applying it
The author's own profile page right after they edited it
qs.e: A trending list is fine a few seconds old. The other three are read-after-write or check-then-act decisions, which must use the primary (or an atomic write).

qs.s: Your app sends a user's reads to the primary for 5 s after any write. Replica lag is normally 50 ms, but during the nightly batch it reaches 40 s. What breaks?
o: Nothing: 5 s is 100× the normal lag
Writes start failing during the batch
Only other users are affected, never the author
After 5 s the author reads from a replica that is 40 s behind and sees their change disappear. The window must follow measured lag, or reads must go to the primary while lag is above budget
qs.e: A fixed window is a guess about lag. Production setups check real lag (or compare a write position such as a Postgres LSN) and fall back to the primary when replicas are behind.

qs.s: Read this withdrawal handler. Which fix makes it correct under replica lag and concurrent requests?

code.title: withdraw.ts

o: Read from the primary instead of the replica; that is enough
Wrap both queries in a try/catch
Use one atomic statement on the primary: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - $1 WHERE id = $2 AND balance >= $1, and treat 0 updated rows as “insufficient funds”
Add a 1-second sleep before the UPDATE so the replica catches up
qs.e: There are two bugs: a stale read from the replica, and a lost update (two requests read the same balance and both write). Reading from the primary fixes only the first. The atomic conditional UPDATE fixes both.

qs.s: The app sends each read to a random replica. Users say comments sometimes appear and then vanish on the next refresh. Read the output.

code.title: pg_stat_replication (on the primary)
code.src:
SELECT application_name, state, replay_lag FROM pg_stat_replication;

 application_name |   state   |   replay_lag
------------------+-----------+-----------------
 replica_a        | streaming | 00:00:00.031
 replica_b        | streaming | 00:00:42.517

o: Monotonic reads are broken: one request hits replica_a (fresh), the next hits replica_b (42 s behind), so time seems to go backwards. Take replica_b out of rotation while its lag is over budget, or pin each session to one replica
The comments were deleted by a moderator
Replica_a is broken because its lag is too low
The primary is losing writes
qs.e: Two replicas with very different lag break the “never go backwards” guarantee. Lag-aware routing (skip replicas over a lag budget) is the usual production fix, plus finding why replica_b is behind (long queries, a big batch, a slow disk).

qs.s: Which statement about linearizability and serializability is correct?
o: They are two names for the same guarantee
Serializable always implies linearizable
Linearizability is about transactions; serializability is about single keys

Serializability says transactions behave as if run one at a time in some order (not necessarily real-time order); linearizability says each single-object operation takes effect at one instant between its start and end, in real time
qs.e: They answer different questions. A serializable database can still serve a slightly stale read in some serial orders, and a linearizable key-value store says nothing about multi-key transactions. “Strict serializability” combines both.

qs.s: Ana removes her boss from the audience of her photo album, then uploads a party photo to it. The boss still sees the photo for a moment. Which guarantee would prevent this?
o: Read-your-writes
Causal consistency: if write B (the upload) happened after write A (the permission change), nobody may see B without also seeing A
Eventual consistency
Monotonic reads
qs.e: Read-your-writes only protects Ana's own view. The problem is that the boss saw an effect before its cause. Causal consistency keeps cause and effect in order for every reader.

interview.q: Which consistency models would you choose for a social feed, a user profile page, and a bank balance? Why?
answer: Feed: eventual consistency is fine; a post appearing a few seconds late for followers is acceptable. Serve from caches and replicas.
Profile: read-your-writes for the owner (route their reads to the primary after a write, or return the new state from the write), eventual for everyone else.
Balance: strong consistency for decisions. Checks and updates happen atomically on the primary, never on a replica or cache.
Monotonic reads everywhere if possible, so users never see data go backwards.
The model is chosen per read path, and the UI is designed for the gap (optimistic updates, “processing” states).
followups: How do you implement read-your-writes with read replicas?
How would you detect stale reads in production?

interview.q: Users report that their edits disappear right after they save, then come back later. How do you debug and fix it?
answer: Suspect the read path after the write: a read replica, a cache, or a CDN serving the old version.
Check replica lag metrics and cache TTLs at the time of the reports; reproduce by writing and immediately reading.
Short-term fix: return the updated object from the write and render it, so the client does not re-read.
Backend fix: read-your-writes routing (primary for a window, or compare a write position such as a Postgres LSN), and invalidate or update the cache on write.
Also check for lost updates: concurrent edits without version checks can overwrite the change, which looks the same to users.
followups: How would you choose the length of the “read from primary” window?
What does an ETag with If-Match protect against?

interview.q: System design: design a collaborative document editor like Google Docs. What consistency does it need, and how do you get it?
answer: Users must be able to type without waiting for the server, so local edits apply immediately (optimistic) and sync in the background.
Concurrent edits must converge to the same document on every client: use operational transformation (with a central server ordering operations) or CRDTs (such as Yjs or Automerge).
Intent matters, not just convergence: inserting text at the same place should keep both inserts.
Presence (cursors) can be eventually consistent and lossy; the document itself must be durable, so the server stores operations or snapshots plus updates.
Offline editing makes it an AP design: accept edits locally, merge when back online.
followups: OT or CRDT: which would you choose and why?
How do you handle permission changes while someone is editing?

one: A monolith is one deployable application. Microservices split it into independently deployable services that own their own data and talk over the network.
an: One big restaurant kitchen versus a food court. The food court lets each stall change its menu independently, but now customers carry trays between stalls and someone must coordinate the whole thing.
how: Microservices are mainly an organisational tool: they let many teams ship independently. Each service owns its database; no reaching into another's tables.
Costs: network calls that fail, distributed transactions, harder debugging (tracing required), versioned contracts, more infrastructure.
Modular monolith: one deployable with strict internal module boundaries. Most of the design benefit, little of the operational cost. A common modern recommendation.
why: "Should we split into microservices?" is a classic lead-level question. The right answer usually depends on team count, not traffic.
trade: A distributed monolith (services that must deploy together and share a DB) has the costs of both and the benefits of neither.

myth.r: A monolith scales horizontally fine. Microservices scale organisations. With one team, they are usually a net loss.

q.s: A 5-engineer startup wants to split its working monolith into 12 microservices to "prepare for scale". Best advice?
o: Do it now, before it is too late
Keep a modular monolith with clear boundaries; extract a service when a specific need appears
Rewrite in Go
Use 50 services
q.e: Clear module boundaries keep the option open without paying distributed-systems costs today.

more: Database per service and data duplication
Synchronous vs asynchronous communication between services
Strangler fig migration from a monolith
lab: Take a monolith you know and draw its likely service boundaries along business capabilities. For each boundary, list which tables it would own and which calls would cross it.
Count the cross-boundary calls for one common user action. That number is the latency and failure tax you would pay.

plain:
A monolith is one application, deployed as one unit. Microservices split the system into many small applications, each owning its own data and deployed independently, talking over the network.

Microservices mostly solve an organisational problem: letting many teams work without blocking each other. They add a lot of technical complexity.
bridge: It is like splitting one React app into micro-frontends: each team deploys independently, but now you have versioning, shared dependencies and integration problems you never had before.

walk.title: What one checkout costs in each style
steps: Monolith: checkout calls cart.getItems(), pricing.calculate(), orders.create() as normal function calls in one database transaction.
Microservices: checkout calls the cart service, pricing service and order service over HTTP.
Each call can be slow or fail. You need timeouts, retries, and a plan when pricing is down.
There is no single transaction across three databases. If order creation fails after payment, you need a compensation step.
In return, the pricing team can deploy five times a day without coordinating with anyone.

terms: A small, independently deployable service owning its data.
Services that must deploy together and share a DB: the worst of both.
Systems tend to mirror the communication structure of the teams building them.
insights: Count the synchronous hops on the hot path. Each one multiplies failure rate and tail latency.
If two services always deploy together, they are one service with a network in the middle.
Without a trace ID on every call, a cross-service bug takes days to find instead of minutes.

prod.summary: In production, microservices need a platform: a pipeline per service, service discovery, tracing, per-service dashboards and on-call, contract tests, and network-failure handling on every call. Seniors justify each service boundary with a real reason (team ownership, a different scaling profile, isolation), watch for the distributed monolith, and count the network calls on the hot path.
checklist: Each service has one owning team, its own database or schema that no other service queries, and its own deploy pipeline.
The hot path has few synchronous hops; a chain deeper than 3–4 services on a user request is a warning.
Every service-to-service call has a timeout, a retry policy and a fallback; the caller's deadline is propagated.
Distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry) covers every service, and every log line carries the trace ID.
Contracts are versioned and tested (consumer-driven contract tests or schema checks), so services really deploy independently.
If two services always deploy together, merge them or fix the boundary.
Cost is tracked per service: idle replicas, load balancers and cross-zone traffic add up.
numbers: Availability multiplies along a synchronous chain: 5 services at 99.9% each give about 99.5% (0.999<sup>5</sup>), before retries or fallbacks.
Fan-out amplifies tail latency: if a request calls 10 services in parallel and each is slow 1% of the time, the request is slow about 9.6% of the time (1 − 0.99<sup>10</sup>).
In 2023 the Prime Video team reported cutting infrastructure cost by over 90% after moving one monitoring service from distributed Step Functions and Lambda components into a single process.
failures: Every release needs 4 services deployed in a fixed order, or the site breaks.
A distributed monolith: shared tables or breaking contract changes. Make changes backward compatible (expand, migrate, contract), give each service its own data, or merge the services.
Product page p99 is 2.5 s; the trace shows 14 sequential service calls.
Chatty boundaries. Run independent calls in parallel, add a BFF or composition layer, cache reference data, or move tightly coupled logic into one service.
Reports show wrong totals after the orders team changed a column type.
The reporting service read the orders tables directly. Share data through an API, events or CDC into a store reporting owns; never share tables between services.
A bug takes 3 days to find because logs are in 9 places with no common ID.
No trace propagation. Add OpenTelemetry with W3C traceparent on every HTTP call and every message, and log the trace ID.

code.title: One shared client for service calls: deadline, timeout, trace context
code.note: A shared client makes the safe behaviour the default: no call without a timeout, no call after the caller's deadline, and every call joins the same trace. On an error status the body is cancelled, because an unread body keeps the connection busy in Node's fetch (undici).

qs.s: Checkout calls 4 services in sequence, each 99.95% available, with no fallbacks. Best estimate of checkout availability?
o: About 99.8%: 0.9995<sup>4</sup>; every extra synchronous hop lowers it
qs.e: Availabilities multiply when every hop must succeed. Four hops lose about 0.2%, which is roughly 17 hours of failures per year instead of about 4.4 for one service.

qs.s: Orders and Invoices are separate services, but they always change together, deploy together and share 6 tables. The team wants to “fix the microservice pain”. Best move?
o: Add a message queue between them
Merge them into one service (or one module), and split again only if a real boundary appears
Put an API gateway in front of both
Give each service its own read replica
qs.e: They are one service in reality. A queue or gateway adds more moving parts without removing the coupling. Boundaries follow independent change, not code size.

qs.s: Reporting needs data from 5 services. Which approach keeps the services independent?
o: Reporting connects read-only to all 5 databases
Reporting calls 5 APIs live for every report page
Services publish events (or CDC) into a reporting store that the reporting team owns
Each service renders its own part of the report
qs.e: Direct database reads couple reporting to every internal schema. Live API calls make reports slow and fragile. A dedicated read store fed by events is the usual answer.

qs.s: Read this trace of a product page. Which change cuts the latency the most?

code.title: trace: GET /product/9 (2,310 ms)
code.src:
GET /product/9                       2310 ms
  catalog  GET /items/9               120 ms   start    0 ms
  pricing  GET /price/9               140 ms   start  120 ms
  stock    GET /stock/9               110 ms   start  260 ms
  reviews  GET /reviews/9            1850 ms   start  370 ms
  recs     GET /recs/9                 90 ms   start 2220 ms
# none of the calls uses data from another call

o: Add more replicas of every service
Run the independent calls in parallel, and give reviews (optional) a short timeout with a fallback. The page then takes about as long as the slowest critical call, around 150 ms
Move all five services into one Kubernetes namespace
Cache the whole page for 24 hours
qs.e: The calls are sequential for no reason, and one optional dependency dominates. Parallel calls turn the sum into the maximum, and the timeout stops reviews from deciding page speed. More replicas do not make a slow sequential chain faster.

qs.s: The orders team plans to deploy this change to a public response on Tuesday. The mobile app and the invoices service read total. What is the safe approach?

code.title: GET /v1/orders/:id (diff)

o: Deploy it and tell the other teams in the release notes
Deploy orders, invoices and mobile at the same time
Move it to /v2 and delete /v1 the same day

Expand and contract: add totalCents next to total, move consumers over, check that nobody reads total any more (logs or contract tests), then remove it. Old mobile app versions may need total for months
qs.e: A removed field is a breaking change. A coordinated deploy is the distributed monolith again, and it cannot include old mobile apps that users never update. Consumer-driven contract tests would have failed this change in CI.

qs.s: Which reason best justifies extracting a part of a monolith into its own service?
o: Video transcoding needs GPU nodes, scales 20× differently from the web API, and one team owns it end to end
The codebase has passed 100,000 lines
A developer wants to try Rust
Microservices are the modern standard
qs.e: Good reasons are concrete: a separate owning team, very different scaling or hardware, or isolation of failures and security. Code size alone can be handled with modules inside the monolith.

qs.s: You need to move search out of a large monolith without a big-bang rewrite. Which approach is the strangler fig pattern?
o: Freeze features for 6 months and rewrite everything as services
Copy the monolith's database to the new service and let both write to it

Put a routing layer in front, send /search to the new service (first a small share of traffic, then all of it), keep everything else in the monolith, and remove the old code once traffic is fully moved
Run the new search service only in staging until it is perfect
qs.e: The strangler fig replaces a system piece by piece behind a stable entry point, so each step is small and reversible. Sharing one database between old and new code recreates the coupling you are trying to remove.

interview.q: When would you move from a monolith to microservices, and when would you advise against it?
answer: Microservices mainly solve an organisational problem: many teams that need to deploy independently. With one or two teams they usually cost more than they give.
Good triggers: separate team ownership, very different scaling or hardware, strong isolation needs (security, compliance, failure blast radius).
Costs: network failures, distributed transactions (sagas), tracing, contract versioning, a platform for deploys and on-call per service.
A modular monolith with enforced boundaries is a strong default; extract services along those boundaries when a trigger appears.
Warning signs of doing it wrong: services that must deploy together, shared tables, long synchronous call chains.
followups: How do you migrate without a big-bang rewrite?
What is a distributed monolith and how do you detect one?

interview.q: How should services communicate? When do you use synchronous calls and when asynchronous messaging?
answer: Synchronous (HTTP/gRPC) when the caller needs the answer now to respond to the user, for example reading a price.
Asynchronous (events, queues) when the caller only needs the work to happen eventually: emails, search indexing, analytics, follow-up steps.
Every synchronous hop lowers availability (availabilities multiply) and adds latency, so keep the hot path short and parallel.
Async needs idempotent consumers, an outbox for reliable publishing, and tracing across the broker.
Every call needs a timeout, a retry policy at one layer, and a fallback or a clear error.
followups: How do you propagate a deadline across services?
gRPC or REST between services?

interview.q: System design: design the backend of an e-commerce site as microservices. How does checkout work across services?
answer: Services by business capability: catalog, pricing, cart, inventory, orders, payments, shipping, notifications; each owns its data.
Checkout as an orchestrated saga: reserve stock, authorise payment, create the order, then capture and ship; each step has a compensation (release, void, cancel).
Payments use idempotency keys; events are published through an outbox; consumers are idempotent.
Read-heavy pages (catalog, search) use caches and read models fed by events, so checkout load does not affect browsing.
Cross-cutting: an API gateway or BFF at the edge, tracing everywhere, per-service SLOs and dashboards.
followups: What happens if payment succeeds but the order service is down?
How do you prevent overselling the last item?

one transaction")]
