videos.why: Sam Newman and Martin Fowler on when not to use microservices.

videos.t: What Are Microservices Really All About? (And When Not To Use It)
videos.why: What microservices are, in five minutes.

one: One deployable app, internally split into modules with explicit public interfaces and no reaching into each other's internals or tables.
an: Departments in one office building with doors and reception desks, rather than an open floor where anyone grabs anything from any desk.
how: Modules (billing, catalog, orders) expose a small API; others call only that. Each module owns its tables.
Enforce boundaries with tooling: lint rules on imports (eslint-plugin-boundaries, dependency-cruiser, Nx module boundaries, ArchUnit), separate packages in a monorepo.

Modules talk by calling the public API or by in-process events. Both stay inside one process, so there is no network failure to handle and one database transaction is still possible when truly needed.
why: Gets the design discipline of services without network calls, distributed transactions or extra infrastructure.
trade: Boundaries erode unless enforced automatically. Shared database transactions across modules are tempting and recreate coupling.

myth.r: Spaghetti comes from missing boundaries, which can happen in microservices too.

q.s: What is the single most important rule for keeping a modular monolith modular?
o: Use one big shared utils folder
Modules interact only through each other's public interfaces, enforced by tooling
Put everything in one file
Share all tables
q.e: Boundaries without enforcement decay within months.

more: Separate schemas per module in one database
Extracting a module into a service
lab: In a TS project, create modules/billing and modules/orders, each with an index.ts public API. Add eslint-plugin-boundaries (or Nx tags) so importing another module's internals fails lint.

plain:
A modular monolith is one application, deployed as one unit, but organised inside into clear modules (billing, catalogue, orders). Each module has a small public interface and owns its own tables. Other modules may only use that interface.

You get clean boundaries and simple operations at the same time.
bridge: It is like a well-organised frontend codebase where each feature folder exports only a few things from its index.ts, and a lint rule stops imports reaching into another feature's internals.

walk.title: Keeping modules honest
steps: Folders: modules/billing, modules/orders, modules/catalog, each with an index.ts public API.
Orders needs a price: it calls catalog.getPrice(productId), not db.products.findUnique directly.
A lint rule (eslint-plugin-boundaries or Nx) fails the build if orders imports catalog/internal/....
Each module's tables are only queried by that module.
A year later, the catalogue needs its own team and scaling. Extracting it into a service is straightforward because the seam already exists.

terms: A part of the codebase with a clear responsibility and public interface.
The small set of functions other modules may call.
A place where the code can be split cleanly.
insights: Boundary rules belong in CI as a required check, not in a wiki page.
Give each module its own Postgres schema early: cross-module joins are the hardest coupling to remove later.
Frequent cross-module transactions mean the boundary is in the wrong place.

prod.summary: In production, a modular monolith is one deploy, one runtime and usually one database, with boundaries enforced by tooling, not by good intentions. Seniors check that boundary rules run in CI, that modules do not read each other's tables, and that the module graph has no cycles. It is the cheapest way to keep the option of extracting a service later.
checklist: Boundary rules run in CI and fail the build (dependency-cruiser, eslint-plugin-boundaries, Nx module boundaries, ArchUnit for Java).
Each module owns its tables, ideally in its own Postgres schema; a database role per module or a review rule stops cross-module SQL.
No circular dependencies between modules; the allowed direction is written down.
Modules talk only through a public API (an index.ts) or in-process events; no deep imports.
Transactions across modules are rare and explicit; if one is needed often, the boundary is probably wrong.
Each module has an owner (CODEOWNERS) and tests that can run on their own.
numbers: An in-process function call costs nanoseconds; a call to another service in the same datacentre costs about 0.5 ms round trip plus serialization, roughly a thousand times more, and it can fail.
Shopify kept its main Rails monolith and split it into components with enforced boundaries (their open-source tool Packwerk) instead of moving to microservices.
failures: A small change in billing breaks the orders page.
Orders imported billing internals or queried billing tables. Expose what orders needs through billing's public API, and turn on the import rule so it cannot happen again.
Extracting the catalog module into a service takes 6 months instead of 6 weeks.
Other modules joined catalog tables directly in SQL. Keep module data private from day one (own schema, no cross-schema joins); expose reads through the module's API or views it owns.
The app crashes at startup with ReferenceError: Cannot access 'X' before initialization.
A circular import between modules. Break the cycle: move the shared type into a small shared kernel, or replace the direct call with an event.
Boundary rules exist, but violations keep appearing on main.
The check runs only locally or only on main. Run it on every pull request as a required status check.

code.title: dependency-cruiser rules: public API only, no cycles
code.note: $1 in pathNot is the module name captured in from.path, so imports inside the same module are allowed, and imports into another module are allowed only through its index.ts.

qs.s: Orders needs the product price. Which call keeps the monolith modular?
o: import { prisma } from '@/db'; prisma.product.findUnique(…) inside the orders module
import { getPrice } from '@/modules/catalog' (catalog's public index)
import { priceRepo } from '@/modules/catalog/internal/repo'
Copy the price logic into the orders module
qs.e: Only the public API is stable. Reading catalog's tables or internals ties orders to catalog's storage details, and copying logic creates two sources of truth.

qs.s: Billing imports orders and orders imports billing. Both are needed. Which change removes the cycle with the least coupling?
o: Merge both modules into one big module
Use dynamic import() to hide the cycle from the linter
Move all shared code into a utils folder
Orders publishes an in-process OrderPlaced event that billing subscribes to, so only billing depends on orders' public types
qs.e: An event reverses one direction of the dependency. Dynamic imports hide the problem, a big utils folder becomes a new dumping ground, and merging gives up the boundary.

qs.s: A modular monolith shares one Postgres database. What gives the strongest protection against modules reading each other's tables?
o: A separate schema per module, each module connecting with its own role that has no grants on other schemas
A comment at the top of each table definition
Table names prefixed with the module name
A wiki page listing table owners
qs.e: Database permissions turn the rule into an error at runtime, like lint rules do for imports. Prefixes and documentation help people, but they do not stop a query.

qs.s: The import-boundary lint passes on this file. What is the boundary problem, and what is the fix?

code.title: src/modules/orders/report.ts

o: No problem: the lint rule passed, so the boundary holds
The query is slow; add an index on invoices.order_id

Orders reads billing's tables directly, which import lint cannot see. Ask billing's public API for invoice statuses by order IDs (or read a view that billing owns), and block it at the database with a role per module
Move the query into a shared utils folder
qs.e: SQL joins are a hidden dependency: billing can no longer change its tables, and extracting billing later breaks this report. Import rules only check code imports, so data boundaries need their own enforcement.

qs.s: CI prints these violations. Which pair of fixes is right?

code.title: npx depcruise src
code.src:
error only-public-api-between-modules: src/modules/shipping/service.ts → src/modules/orders/internal/repo.ts
  error no-circular: src/modules/orders/index.ts → 
      src/modules/billing/index.ts →
      src/modules/orders/index.ts

x 2 dependency violations (2 errors, 0 warnings). 312 modules, 801 dependencies cruised.

o: Break the cycle by making one direction an in-process event (or moving the shared type into a small shared kernel), and make shipping call a function exported from orders/index.ts
Mark both rules as warnings so the build passes
Merge orders, billing and shipping into one module
Use dynamic import() in both places so the tool cannot see the imports
qs.e: Each error has a design fix. Turning rules into warnings or hiding imports keeps the coupling and only removes the alarm. Merging everything gives up the boundaries the rules exist to protect.

qs.s: In a modular monolith with one Postgres database, placing an order must also create an invoice. The team wraps both modules' calls in one database transaction. What is the honest trade-off?
o: There is no downside: one transaction is always best
It is wrong: modules must never share a transaction
It is slower than a saga
It is simple and correct today, but it couples the two modules: if billing is ever extracted into a service, this flow needs an outbox and a saga instead. Keep such transactions few and explicit
qs.e: Using the database's atomicity is a real advantage of a monolith. The price is that the seam is not clean. Senior answers name both sides instead of following a rule blindly.

qs.s: A heavy image-processing module in the monolith uses a lot of CPU at night and slows the web API. What is the lightest fix?
o: Rewrite image processing as a microservice in another language
Run the same codebase as two process types: web pods that serve HTTP, and worker pods that run only the image jobs from a queue. Scale and limit them separately
Give the web pods more CPU
Run image processing only on weekends
qs.e: One codebase does not mean one process type. Separate entry points (web, worker, scheduler) give resource isolation and separate scaling without network contracts between modules.

interview.q: What is a modular monolith, and how is it different from a normal monolith and from microservices?
answer: One deployable and usually one database, but split into modules with small public APIs and private internals and tables.
Compared to a tangled monolith: boundaries are explicit and enforced by tools, so changes stay local.
Compared to microservices: in-process calls (fast, no partial failure), real database transactions, one deploy pipeline, much less infrastructure.
Limits: one deploy unit (a bad change can take down everything), shared runtime resources, and scaling is for the whole app (unless you run separate process types).
It keeps the option to extract a service later, because the seams already exist.
followups: How do modules communicate?
When would you extract a module into a service?

interview.q: How do you enforce module boundaries so they survive two years and twenty engineers?
answer: Import rules in CI as a required check: dependency-cruiser, eslint-plugin-boundaries or Nx tags in TypeScript; ArchUnit in Java; Packwerk in Ruby.
Data rules: a schema per module and a database role per module, or at least a review rule against cross-module SQL.
No cycles: define the allowed direction of dependencies and use events to reverse one direction when needed.
Ownership: CODEOWNERS per module and module-level tests.
Track violations as a number that only goes down; allow a temporary allowlist for legacy code instead of switching the rule off.
followups: How do you handle code that every module needs?
How would you introduce these rules into an existing codebase?

interview.q: You inherit a 300,000-line monolith with no boundaries. How do you make it modular without stopping feature work?
answer: Map the domain first: find business capabilities and the tables each one really uses (query logs help).
Choose one boundary with high value and clear ownership; create its module folder with a public API, and move code behind it step by step.
Turn on the boundary rule for that module only, with an allowlist of existing violations that must shrink over time.
Move data ownership: stop other modules writing its tables first, then reading them.
Repeat module by module; measure progress (violations, build and test times) and keep shipping features in parallel.
followups: How do you convince product managers to invest in this?
What would make you choose a rewrite instead?

videos.why: Simon Brown's talk that made the modular monolith popular.

videos.t: You’re Building Modular Monoliths All Wrong
videos.why: Common mistakes when drawing module boundaries.

one: A single entry point in front of backend services that handles routing, auth, rate limits, API keys and request shaping.
an: An embassy front desk: checks your documents once, then sends you to the right office.
how: Clients call api.acme.com; the gateway routes /orders to the orders service, /users to users.
Cross-cutting features: JWT validation, quotas per API key, request/response transformation, caching, logging.
Products: Kong, AWS API Gateway, Apigee, Envoy-based gateways, Kubernetes Gateway API implementations.
why: Without it, every service reimplements auth and rate limiting, and clients must know the internal topology.
trade: It can become a bottleneck or a dumping ground for business logic. Keep it about traffic policy, not domain rules.

myth.m: The gateway authorizes everything, so services do not need checks.
myth.r: The gateway can authenticate. Fine-grained authorization (may this user see this order?) belongs in the service that owns the data.

q.s: What should NOT live in an API gateway?
o: Rate limiting
Routing
Whether a customer may cancel an order after shipping
API key validation
q.e: That is a business rule owned by the order domain.

more: Gateway vs BFF vs service mesh
Gateway as a single point of failure
lab: Run Kong or Traefik in Docker in front of two small services; route by path, add a rate limit plugin and API key auth, then hit it with curl.

plain: An API gateway is the single front door for many backend services. Clients call one address; the gateway routes each request to the right service and handles shared jobs like checking API keys, rate limiting and logging.
bridge: Your Vite dev proxy routes /api to one backend. An API gateway does that for many services, plus security and traffic rules.

walk.title: One request through a gateway
steps: Client calls GET https://api.shop.com/orders/9 with an API key.
Gateway checks the key is valid and the client is under its rate limit.
It validates the JWT and adds the user ID as a header.
Routing rule: /orders/* → orders service. The request is forwarded.
The orders service still checks that order 9 belongs to this user. The gateway does not know business rules.

terms: A front door that routes and applies shared policies.
Choosing which backend handles a request.
An identifier for a client application.
Usage limit per client over a period.
insights: Check the gateway's defaults on day one: timeouts, retries and rate-limit counters are often unsafe for production.
Treat gateway config like code: review, validation in CI, canary rollout, instant rollback.
Make the gateway the only way in. If services are reachable directly, its checks can be skipped.

prod.summary: In production the gateway is the most shared piece of infrastructure you run: every request passes through it, so its timeouts, retries and limits decide how failures spread. Seniors keep it thin (routing, authentication, quotas, logging), run several stateless replicas, and treat its config like code, with review, tests and fast rollback.
checklist: Timeouts are set per route: shorter than the client's timeout, longer than the backend's normal p99. Kong's default of 60 s for connect, read and write is far too long for most APIs.
Gateway retries are off for non-idempotent methods (POST, PATCH) unless the route requires an Idempotency-Key. Kong retries a failed proxy attempt 5 times by default.
Rate-limit counters are shared across gateway replicas (Redis or a cluster policy), or the per-node limit is divided by the number of replicas.
JWT checks cover signature, exp, iss and aud; signing keys (JWKS) are cached; incoming identity headers such as X-User-Id are stripped before the gateway sets its own.
Backends accept traffic only from the gateway (private network, network policy or mTLS), so nobody can skip the gateway's checks by calling a service directly.
Every request gets a request ID and a traceparent header; access logs include route, upstream, status and upstream latency.
At least 2–3 gateway replicas across zones, config validated in CI, and a known-good config that can be restored in minutes.
numbers: AWS API Gateway REST APIs: integration timeout 50 ms–29 s by default (Regional and private APIs can request more, possibly with a lower throttle quota); max payload 10 MB.
AWS API Gateway account default: 10,000 requests per second per Region with a burst bucket of 5,000 (2,500/1,250 in some newer Regions).
Kong Gateway service defaults: retries 5; connect_timeout, read_timeout and write_timeout 60,000 ms. The Rate Limiting plugin's default policy is local (counters in each node's memory).
The community Kubernetes ingress-nginx controller was retired in March 2026 (no more fixes); new clusters usually pick a Gateway API implementation.
failures: Report export fails with 504 Gateway Timeout after exactly 29 s, but the service logs show success at 40 s.

The gateway timeout (AWS REST default max 29 s) is shorter than the slow endpoint. Do not just raise it: make long work asynchronous (202 Accepted plus a job ID, then poll or webhook) and keep gateway timeouts tight.
One POST /payments sometimes creates 2–3 charges, always during backend deploys.

The gateway retried requests whose first attempt had already reached the backend (Kong retries 5 times by default). Disable gateway retries on non-idempotent routes, or require an Idempotency-Key that the service deduplicates.
A client on a 100 requests/minute plan actually gets about 300 per minute.

The rate limiter uses per-node counters and there are 3 gateway replicas behind the load balancer. Use a shared counter store (Redis), or set the per-node limit to plan ÷ replicas and accept that it is approximate.
A pentest shows that sending X-User-Id: 1 to the public API lets anyone act as user 1.
The gateway forwarded a client-supplied trusted header. Strip all internal identity headers from incoming requests and set them only after the token is verified.
Every API returns 404 for 20 minutes after a gateway config change, while all services are healthy.
The gateway is a shared single point of failure. Validate config in CI, roll it out to one replica first (canary), and keep the last known-good config ready for instant rollback.

code.title: Kong declarative config: safe timeouts, no blind retries, shared rate limit
code.note: Each commented line overrides a default that hurts in production: 60 s timeouts, 5 retries, and per-node rate-limit counters.
code.src:
_format_version: "3.0"
services:
  - name: orders
    url: http://orders.internal:8080
    connect_timeout: 1000   # Kong default: 60000 ms
    read_timeout: 5000      # below the client's timeout
    write_timeout: 5000
    retries: 0              # Kong default: 5 (unsafe for POST)
    routes:
      - name: orders
        paths: ["/orders"]
        strip_path: false
    plugins:
      - name: key-auth
      - name: rate-limiting
        config:
          minute: 600
          policy: redis      # default "local" counts per gateway node
          redis:
            host: redis.internal
            port: 6379

qs.s: The mobile app times out after 10 s. The gateway's upstream timeout is 30 s and the orders service has no timeout on its database calls. The database hangs. What happens?
o: Users wait 30 s and then see a clean 504 from the gateway
Nothing bad: each layer's timeout is independent
The app gives up at 10 s (and users often tap retry), while the gateway and service keep working on requests nobody waits for. Timeouts should get shorter as you go deeper
The gateway reads the app's timeout from the request and stops at 10 s automatically
qs.e: Timeouts must shrink from the outside in: client > gateway > service > database. Otherwise inner layers waste capacity on abandoned requests, and user retries add more load. Nothing passes the client's timeout down unless you send a deadline header yourself.

qs.s: Gateway access log for 3% of requests, only during deploys of the orders service: route=orders status=502 upstream_status=- upstream_connect_time=-. Most likely cause?
o: The gateway still sends traffic to pods that are already shutting down; the orders service needs graceful shutdown (fail readiness, short delay, drain)
The JWT signing key rotated during the deploy
The client exceeded its rate limit
The client sent an invalid JSON body
qs.e: No upstream status and no connect time means the gateway could not reach a backend at all. During deploys that usually means pods stop before the endpoint list is updated. Rate limiting gives 429, and bad bodies give 4xx from the service itself.

qs.s: A plan allows 1,200 requests per minute per API key. You run 4 gateway replicas with per-node (local) counters behind round-robin. What should you do?
o: Set 1,200 per node; round-robin makes it exact
Set 4,800 per node to be safe
Set 300 per node; this is exact under any load balancer
Set 300 per node, knowing it is only approximate: traffic is never perfectly even, and scaling to 6 replicas silently raises the real limit to 1,800. Use a shared store if the limit matters
qs.e: Local counters are cheap but each node only sees its own share. 1,200 ÷ 4 = 300 works on average, but the real limit changes with replica count and uneven routing. Paid quotas usually need a shared counter (Redis).

qs.s: You deploy this route for a canary of orders v2, which changes the response format. What will users notice?

code.title: httproute.yaml (Kubernetes Gateway API)
code.src:
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: orders
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - name: public-gw
  rules:
    - matches:
        - path: { type: PathPrefix, value: /orders }
      backendRefs:
        - { name: orders-v1, port: 8080, weight: 90 }
        - { name: orders-v2, port: 8080, weight: 10 }

o: Exactly 10% of users see v2; the others never do

About 10% of requests go to v2, chosen per request, so one user can switch between v1 and v2 on every page load. With a changed format the UI can break; keep v2 backward compatible, or split by a header or cookie so each user stays on one version
v2 only gets traffic when v1 fails
The first 10 requests per minute go to v2
qs.e: Weights split requests, not users. That is fine for compatible changes and dangerous for format changes. Matching on a header (for example a canary cookie set by the edge) keeps a user on one version.

qs.s: At 09:00 the identity provider rotated its signing keys. Since then, every request with a new token fails at the gateway. Read the log.

code.title: gateway.log
code.src:
09:00:12Z gw status=401 route=orders err="jwt: no key found for kid=2026-10-b"
09:00:12Z gw jwks_cache age=21h ttl=24h keys=[2026-09-a]
09:00:13Z gw status=200 route=orders kid=2026-09-a
09:00:13Z gw status=401 route=users err="jwt: no key found for kid=2026-10-b"

o: The new tokens are forged; block the users
Increase the JWKS cache TTL to 7 days
Turn off signature checks until the cache expires

The gateway cached the key set (JWKS) and does not refresh it when it sees an unknown kid. Refetch the JWKS on an unknown kid (rate-limited), use a shorter TTL, and ask the provider to publish new keys before signing with them
qs.e: Key rotation works only if verifiers learn new keys quickly. The standard pattern is “unknown kid → refresh once, then decide”. A longer cache makes it worse, and disabling checks is a security hole.

qs.s: Your gateway config has grown 40 rules that reshape responses differently for iOS, Android and web. Every client change needs a gateway change. What is the better structure?
o: A backend-for-frontend (BFF) per client type that shapes data for its screens, owned by that client team, while the gateway stays thin (routing, auth, quotas)
Move the 40 rules into Lua plugins inside the gateway
Make every backend service return all three formats
Ask clients to accept one generic format and do more requests
qs.e: Client-specific shaping is product logic that changes often, so it belongs with the team that owns the client. Plugins only hide the same coupling in a harder-to-test place.

qs.s: The gateway limits each API key to 100 requests per fixed minute (counter resets at :00). A client sends 100 requests at 10:00:59 and 100 more at 10:01:00. What happens, and what limits bursts better?
o: The second 100 are rejected
Only 100 of the 200 requests reach the backend
All 200 pass within 2 seconds, because they fall in two different windows. A sliding window or a token bucket (rate plus a burst size) limits this
The client is banned for one minute
qs.e: Fixed windows are cheap but allow up to 2× the limit around the boundary. Sliding-window counters smooth this; a token bucket makes the allowed burst an explicit setting.

interview.q: What belongs in an API gateway, and what should stay out?
answer: In: routing, TLS termination, authentication (token validation), API keys and quotas, rate limiting, request size limits, request IDs and tracing headers, access logs.
Out: business rules and fine-grained authorization (“may this user cancel this order?”) belong in the service that owns the data.
Client-specific response shaping belongs in BFFs, not in gateway plugins.
Gateway timeouts and retries must fit the system: timeouts shrink from the outside in, and no blind retries of non-idempotent requests.
Strip client-supplied identity headers; backends must be reachable only through the gateway or verify identity themselves.
followups: Gateway vs service mesh: what is the difference?
Where would you validate JWTs, and why?

interview.q: System design: design a rate limiter for a public API that runs on many gateway nodes.
answer: Clarify the rule: per API key, per user or per IP; per second or per day; hard limit or soft; which response (429 with Retry-After and rate-limit headers).
Algorithm: token bucket (rate + burst) or sliding-window counter; fixed windows allow double bursts at the boundary.
State: a shared store such as Redis with atomic operations (a Lua script or INCR with expiry), or local counters divided by node count when approximate is fine.
Failure mode: decide whether to fail open (allow) or closed (reject) when Redis is down; usually fail open with a local fallback limit.
Scale: shard counters by key, keep the hot path to one round trip, and monitor rejected requests per key.
followups: How do you handle a client spread over many IP addresses?
How do you make the limit accurate across regions?

interview.q: The gateway is a single point of failure. How do you run it so it is not one?
answer: Several stateless replicas across zones behind a load balancer, with autoscaling and enough headroom to lose a zone.
Configuration as code: validated in CI, rolled out gradually (one replica or one percent first), with a known-good version ready for instant rollback.
Shared state (rate-limit counters, JWKS) must degrade safely when its store is slow or down.
Health checks and SLOs for the gateway itself (latency added, 5xx it generates versus upstream 5xx).
Keep it thin: every feature added to the gateway is a new way to take down every API at once.
followups: How would you test a gateway config change before production?
What metrics show the gateway, not a backend, is the problem?

one: A durable buffer where producers drop messages and consumers process them later, at their own pace.
an: An order rail in a kitchen. Waiters clip tickets on; cooks take them when ready. A rush does not crush the cooks; the rail just gets longer.
how: Producer → queue → consumer. Each message is processed by one consumer in a group, then acknowledged. Unacked messages are redelivered after a timeout.
Delivery semantics: at-most-once (may lose), at-least-once (may duplicate, the usual choice), "exactly-once" (only within specific systems, in practice achieved with idempotent consumers).
Tools: RabbitMQ, SQS, Redis-based queues, NATS, and Kafka used as a queue.
why: Decouples services in time: the producer does not wait, spikes are smoothed, and consumer outages do not lose work.
trade: Ordering is often not guaranteed (or only per partition/group). Duplicates must be handled. Monitor queue depth and age, and set up a dead-letter queue for poison messages.

myth.m: The queue guarantees each message is processed exactly once.
myth.r: Design consumers to be idempotent. Redelivery happens after crashes, timeouts and network glitches.

q.s: A consumer crashes after charging a card but before acking the message. What happens next, and what protects you?
o: The message is lost; nothing needed
It is redelivered; an idempotency key on the charge prevents a double charge
The queue rolls back the charge
Kafka handles it
q.e: At-least-once delivery plus idempotent side effects is the standard combination.

more: Queue depth and age as health metrics
lab: Run RabbitMQ in Docker and follow its first three official tutorials in your language.
Make a consumer crash before acknowledging and watch the message get redelivered.
Add a dead-letter queue and route messages there after 3 failures.

plain:
A message queue lets one part of the system leave work for another part to do later. The sender puts a message in the queue and moves on. A consumer takes messages one by one, processes them, and confirms each one.

If the consumer is slow or down, messages wait in the queue instead of being lost.
bridge: It is like a to-do list shared between programs. Background job libraries (BullMQ, Sidekiq) are built on top of queues.

walk.title: A crash in the middle of processing
steps: Message: “charge order 42”. The consumer takes it. The queue hides it from other consumers for 30 seconds.
The consumer charges the card, then crashes before confirming (acknowledging) the message.
After 30 seconds without confirmation, the queue makes the message visible again. Another consumer takes it.
Without protection, the card is charged twice. With an idempotency key per order, the second charge is recognised and skipped.
The consumer confirms the message; it is removed from the queue.

terms: Who sends messages / who processes them.
Telling the queue a message is done so it can be deleted.
Every message is delivered, possibly more than once.
Where messages go after failing too many times.
insights: Alert on the age of the oldest message, not only on queue length.
The visibility or ack timeout must be longer than the slowest normal job, or healthy jobs run twice.
A DLQ without an alarm and a redrive runbook is where messages go to be forgotten.

prod.summary: In production, a queue is healthy when two numbers are boring: how many messages are waiting, and how old the oldest one is. Seniors set visibility or ack timeouts longer than the worst normal processing time, cap redeliveries into a dead-letter queue, make consumers idempotent, and keep a tested runbook for redriving the DLQ.
checklist: The visibility timeout (SQS) or ack timeout is longer than the slowest normal job, or the consumer extends it while working (ChangeMessageVisibility).
A dead-letter queue with a redelivery cap (SQS maxReceiveCount, RabbitMQ delivery-limit), an alarm on DLQ depth > 0, and a tested redrive procedure.
Consumers are idempotent (dedup by message ID or business key) and ack only after the side effect is committed.
Alarms on the age of the oldest message (SQS ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage), not only on queue length.
Prefetch and concurrency are bounded (RabbitMQ basic.qos prefetch, SQS batch size), so one consumer does not hoard messages.
Messages stay small; large payloads go to object storage with a pointer in the message.
Producers handle a broker outage (outbox, or retries with backoff) instead of fire-and-forget.
numbers: Amazon SQS: default visibility timeout 30 s (max 12 hours); retention 4 days by default (max 14 days); max message size 1 MiB; long polling waits up to 20 s.
SQS FIFO without high-throughput mode: 300 API calls per second per action, or 3,000 messages per second with batches of 10.
RabbitMQ 4.0+: quorum queues have a default delivery-limit of 20, after which a message is dropped or dead-lettered.
RabbitMQ consumer_timeout defaults to 30 minutes: an unacked delivery older than that closes the channel with PRECONDITION_FAILED and its messages are requeued.
failures: The same job runs 2–3 times; logs show each run takes about 45 s.

Processing (45 s) is longer than the SQS visibility timeout (30 s default), so the message becomes visible again and another worker takes it. Raise the timeout well above processing time or extend it with a heartbeat, and make the job idempotent.
Queue length is flat but ApproximateAgeOfOldestMessage keeps rising into hours.
A poison message fails forever (and in a FIFO group it blocks everything behind it). Set maxReceiveCount (for example 5) with a DLQ and alert on DLQ depth.
RabbitMQ consumers lose their channel with PRECONDITION_FAILED … “timed out waiting for a consumer acknowledgement”.
A long task holds a delivery longer than consumer_timeout (30 min default). Split the job, ack and track progress elsewhere, or raise the timeout for that queue only.
Consumers sit at 10% CPU while the queue grows at peak.
Consumers are I/O-bound with concurrency 1 or a tiny prefetch. Raise per-consumer concurrency, and autoscale consumers on queue age or backlog (KEDA, SQS-based scaling), not on CPU.
After a DLQ redrive, some customers get duplicate refunds.
Some messages had partly succeeded before failing. Make handlers idempotent before redriving, and redrive in small batches while watching errors.

code.title: SQS consumer: long polling, heartbeat, ack after success
code.note: Deleting the message is the ack, so it happens only after handle() succeeds. Failed messages are not deleted; the redrive policy moves them to the DLQ after maxReceiveCount tries.

qs.s: A queue receives 200 messages/s. Each consumer handles 25 messages/s. After an outage there is a backlog of 360,000 messages. With 12 consumers, how long until the backlog is gone?
o: About 1 hour: 12 × 25 = 300/s, minus 200/s still arriving = 100/s net; 360,000 ÷ 100 = 3,600 s
About 20 minutes
About 2 hours
It never drains
qs.e: The tempting answer, 20 minutes (360,000 ÷ 300), forgets that new messages keep arriving. Only the spare capacity drains the backlog. This is why you keep consumer headroom.

qs.s: On SQS, all events of one customer must be processed in order, but different customers may be processed in parallel. What do you use?
o: A standard queue with a single consumer
A standard queue, sorting messages by timestamp in the consumer
A FIFO queue with MessageGroupId = customerId
One standard queue per consumer instance
qs.e: FIFO queues keep order within a message group and process different groups in parallel. A single consumer gives order but no parallelism, and sorting in the consumer cannot fix messages that have not arrived yet.

qs.s: A consumer does: (1) delete the message, (2) charge the card. Which delivery guarantee does the charge get?
o: At-least-once
Exactly-once
Strict ordering
At-most-once: if the process crashes between the delete and the charge, the charge never happens
qs.e: Acking before the work means a crash loses the work. Acking after the work gives at-least-once, and then the charge needs an idempotency key so a redelivery does not charge twice.

qs.s: Three consumers start one after another, a few seconds apart. The queue already holds 10,000 messages; each takes about 2 s. What happens?

code.title: worker.ts (amqplib)

o: RabbitMQ gives each consumer one message at a time, so the work is shared evenly
The messages are processed in parallel at full speed

Without a prefetch limit, the first consumer receives (almost) all messages into its buffer while the others sit idle. Its memory grows, and if it crashes everything is redelivered at once. Set ch.prefetch(10) or similar
Messages are lost because they are not acknowledged in time
qs.e: Prefetch (basic.qos) limits how many unacknowledged messages one consumer can hold. The default is unlimited, so the earliest consumer hoards the backlog. A small prefetch spreads work across consumers.

qs.s: Read this SQS redrive policy. What is the risk?

code.title: RedrivePolicy

o: A single temporary failure (a timeout, a deploy, a visibility timeout that expired) sends a healthy message straight to the DLQ. Use 3–5 so transient errors get retried, and keep the DLQ for real poison messages
Messages are retried forever
The DLQ is never used
Messages are deleted after one read
qs.e: maxReceiveCount counts receives, not real failures. With 1, there are no retries at all, so the DLQ fills with messages that would have succeeded on the second try.

qs.s: When is a message queue the WRONG choice?
o: Sending welcome emails after signup
Resizing uploaded images
Absorbing a traffic spike of webhook events
Calculating a shipping price that the checkout page must show right now
qs.e: If the user is waiting for the answer, a queue only adds latency and complexity: you would need to wait for a reply anyway. Queues fit work that can happen later.

qs.s: A standard (non-FIFO) queue with 5 competing consumers receives “status = SHIPPED” and then “status = DELIVERED” for the same order. Sometimes the final status is SHIPPED. Why, and what is a good fix?
o: The queue lost the DELIVERED message

Two consumers processed the messages in parallel and the older one finished last. Include a version or timestamp and update only if it is newer (WHERE version < $new), or use FIFO grouping by order ID
The database does not support concurrent updates
Consumers must process messages in alphabetical order
qs.e: Competing consumers break ordering even when the queue delivers in order. A version check makes the consumer safe in any order, which also protects against redeliveries.

interview.q: Explain at-most-once, at-least-once and exactly-once delivery. How do you get effectively-once processing?
answer: At-most-once: acknowledge before processing; a crash loses the message.
At-least-once: acknowledge after processing; a crash or timeout causes redelivery, so duplicates happen. This is the normal choice.
Exactly-once delivery across a network is not possible in general; brokers offer it only inside their own system (for example Kafka transactions for read-process-write within Kafka).
Effectively-once = at-least-once + idempotent consumer: dedupe on a message ID or business key in the same transaction as the effect, or use upserts and conditional updates.
For external side effects (payments, emails), pass an idempotency key to the provider.
followups: Where do you store processed message IDs and for how long?
What happens if the dedupe store is down?

interview.q: System design: design a notification system that sends email, SMS and push messages to millions of users.
answer: API accepts a notification request, validates it, stores it, and puts it on a queue; it returns quickly (202).
Separate queues and worker pools per channel (email, SMS, push), so a slow SMS provider does not block push.
Workers respect user preferences, quiet hours and per-provider rate limits; failures retry with backoff, then go to a DLQ.
Idempotency key per notification so redeliveries do not send twice; dedupe and batching for noisy events.
Priorities (password reset before marketing), metrics on queue age per channel, and provider fallback for critical messages.
followups: How do you send a campaign to 10 million users without hitting provider limits?
How do you track delivery and open status?

interview.q: How do you operate a queue in production? What do you monitor and alert on?
answer: Age of the oldest message (users feel delay) and queue depth trend; alert on age above the business SLA.
DLQ depth above zero, with an owner and a tested redrive procedure.
Consumer throughput, error rate and redelivery count; visibility or ack timeout longer than the slowest normal job.
Autoscale consumers on backlog or age, not CPU, with a cap that protects downstream systems (database connections).
Producer side: publish errors and broker availability; an outbox or retries so publishing does not silently fail.
followups: How do you safely redrive 50,000 DLQ messages?
How do you find a poison message?

diagrams.title: Crash before ack: redelivery and an idempotency key
diagrams.src:
sequenceDiagram

  participant A as Consumer A
  participant B as Consumer B
  participant P as Payments
  A->>Q: receive charge order 42
  Note over Q: message hidden for 30 s
  A->>P: charge, key order-42
  P-->>A: charged
  Note over A: crashes before ack
  Note over Q: 30 s pass with no ack, message visible again
  B->>Q: receive the same message
  B->>P: charge, key order-42
  P-->>B: already done, same result
  B->>Q: ack, message deleted
diagrams.caption: What to notice: the queue did its job. It redelivered because it never got an ack. Only the idempotency key stops the second charge.

videos.t: What is a Message Queue?
videos.why: What a message queue is, from the ground up.

one: Publishers emit events to a topic; many independent subscribers each receive them. Streaming platforms like Kafka also keep the events as a replayable log.
an: A queue is a to-do list where each task is done once. Pub/sub is a newspaper: one edition, many readers, each doing their own thing with it. Kafka is a newspaper archive you can reread from any date.
how: Queue vs pub/sub: in a queue, each message goes to one consumer. In pub/sub, every subscriber (in Kafka, every consumer group) gets every event; inside one group the work is split.
Kafka: topics split into partitions (ordered within each partition, keyed e.g. by orderId), retained for days or forever. Consumer groups track their offset and can replay history.
Others: Google Pub/Sub, SNS, NATS, Redis Streams, RabbitMQ exchanges.
why: Adding a new consumer requires no change to the producer. Logs enable rebuilding read models, analytics pipelines and auditing.
trade: Harder to follow what happens after an event (no single call stack). Event schemas become public contracts that need versioning. Kafka is heavy to operate; managed offerings help.

myth.m: Kafka is just a faster queue.
myth.r: Its core idea is a durable, replayable, partitioned log. That enables things queues cannot do, and costs things queues do not.

q.s: Ordering per order matters (Created must be processed before Paid). How do you get that in Kafka?
o: Use one global partition
Use orderId as the message key so all events for one order go to the same partition
Sort by timestamp in the consumer
It is automatic for any key
q.e: Kafka guarantees order within a partition. Keying by entity keeps each entity's events in order while still scaling across partitions.

more: Exactly-once semantics in Kafka (and its limits)
lab: Run Redpanda (Kafka-compatible, simpler) in Docker. Create a topic with 3 partitions.
Produce events keyed by orderId and consume with two consumers in one group; see partitions split between them.
Reset the group's offset to the beginning and replay everything.

plain:
With pub/sub, a publisher announces an event (“order placed”) to a topic, and every subscriber gets its own copy. The publisher does not know or care who listens.

Kafka is a popular event platform that also keeps all events in order for days or forever, so new consumers can read history and others can replay it.
bridge: It is addEventListener at system scale: one event is dispatched, many independent listeners react, and adding a new listener does not change the dispatcher.

walk.title: One event, four reactions
steps: The order service publishes OrderPlaced { orderId: 42, total: 120 } to the orders topic.
The email service sends a confirmation. The inventory service reserves stock. Analytics records revenue. The loyalty service adds points.
Six months later, a fraud-check team subscribes too. The order service code does not change at all.
With Kafka, the fraud team can also replay the last 30 days of OrderPlaced events to train their model.
Events for the same order use the order ID as key, so they stay in order (Placed before Paid before Shipped).

terms: Who sends events / who receives them.
A slice of a Kafka topic; order is guaranteed within a partition.
A consumer's position in the stream.
Consumers sharing the work of one subscription.
insights: Choose the partition key and partition count early; changing either later breaks per-key ordering.
Alert on consumer lag in seconds, per group, not only in message counts.
Retention must outlast your worst consumer outage, or that consumer silently loses events.

prod.summary: In production, Kafka-style pub/sub is about partitions, keys, consumer lag and retention. Seniors choose the partition key for ordering and even load, size the partition count for future consumer parallelism (adding partitions later remaps keys), configure replication for durability, and alert on consumer lag measured in time, not just in messages.
checklist: The partition key gives the ordering you need (for example orderId) and spreads load; no single key carries a big share of traffic.
Partition count is planned for growth: a group can use at most one consumer per partition, and adding partitions changes which partition a key maps to.
Durability: replication factor 3, min.insync.replicas=2, producer acks=all with idempotence on.
Consumers commit offsets after processing (no timer-based auto-commit for side-effecting work) and are idempotent.
Consumer lag is alerted per group, ideally as time lag (seconds behind).
Retention is longer than your worst realistic consumer outage plus any replay needs.
Schemas are registered and checked for compatibility before a producer deploys.
numbers: Kafka defaults: log.retention.hours=168 (7 days), num.partitions=1, broker message.max.bytes 1,048,588 (about 1 MB); producer acks=all since Kafka 3.0.
Kafka consumer: max.poll.interval.ms 300,000 (5 min) and max.poll.records 500. If processing between polls takes longer, the consumer leaves the group and its partitions are rebalanced.
Kafka consumer auto.offset.reset defaults to latest: a new group starts at the end and does not read history unless you set earliest.
Kafka 4.0 (2025) removed ZooKeeper; clusters run in KRaft mode only.
failures: The consumer group keeps rebalancing; logs mention that the poll timeout expired and max.poll.interval.ms.
Processing up to 500 records takes longer than 5 minutes. Lower max.poll.records, speed up processing, or hand slow work to a separate pool and pause the partition meanwhile.
A new analytics consumer shows only today's events, no history.
New groups start at latest by default. Set auto.offset.reset=earliest for the first run, and check that retention still holds the history you need.
One partition has 2 million messages of lag; the other 11 are near zero.
A hot key: one tenant produces most events and they all go to one partition. Use a finer key (for example tenant + entity) or split known hot keys.
After increasing partitions from 6 to 12, some orders are processed out of order.
The key-to-partition mapping changed, so new events for an old key went to a different partition than older ones still in flight. Choose partition counts up front, or drain before changing.
Messages were lost after a broker failure, even though the producer got success responses.
The producer used acks=1 (or min.insync.replicas=1): the leader acknowledged and died before followers copied. Use acks=all with min.insync.replicas=2 and replication factor 3.

code.title: Kafka topic, producer and consumer settings that matter
code.note: auto.offset.reset and enable.auto.commit are the two defaults that surprise teams most: one hides history from new groups, the other can commit offsets for work that never finished.
code.src:
# Topic: 12 partitions (room for 12 parallel consumers), 3 copies of each
kafka-topics.sh --create --topic orders --partitions 12 \
  --replication-factor 3 --config min.insync.replicas=2

# producer.properties
acks=all                     # default since Kafka 3.0: wait for in-sync replicas
enable.idempotence=true      # producer retries cannot create duplicates
compression.type=zstd

# consumer.properties
group.id=billing             # each group gets its own copy of every event
enable.auto.commit=false     # commit offsets after processing, not on a timer
auto.offset.reset=earliest   # a new group reads history (default: latest)
max.poll.records=100         # default 500; smaller batches finish inside...
max.poll.interval.ms=300000  # ...this limit (default 5 min) or the group rebalances
isolation.level=read_committed

qs.s: A topic has 6 partitions. You run 10 consumers in one consumer group to go faster. What happens?
o: Each consumer gets 0.6 partitions and throughput rises by 10/6
Kafka creates 4 more partitions automatically
6 consumers get one partition each and 4 sit idle: parallelism inside a group is capped by the partition count
All 10 consumers read every message
qs.e: Within a group, each partition is assigned to at most one consumer. Extra consumers are only standbys. To scale further you need more partitions, planned in advance.

qs.s: The email service and the analytics service both need every OrderPlaced event. How should they consume?
o: Each uses its own consumer group; every group receives every message
They share one consumer group to split the load
Analytics reads the email service's database
The producer publishes every event twice
qs.e: Consumer groups are how Kafka does pub/sub: groups are independent subscribers. Consumers inside one group share (split) the work, so sharing a group would give each service only part of the events.

qs.s: Consumer code: for (const msg of batch) await sendEmail(msg), with enable.auto.commit=true. The process crashes in the middle of a batch. What is the risk?
o: None: Kafka retries automatically

Depending on the client and timing, offsets may already be committed for messages not yet processed (those emails are never sent), or not yet committed for ones already sent (those are sent again). Commit manually after processing and make sends idempotent
Kafka deletes the batch from the topic
The partition is blocked until an operator resets it
qs.e: Auto-commit runs on a timer (or on the next poll), not when your side effect finishes. For work with side effects, commit after processing and accept at-least-once, with idempotent handlers.

billing  orders  2          880113          1201977         321864   billing-3
billing  orders  3          1203410         1203433         23       billing-1

o: Add more partitions to the topic
Restart all consumers in the group
Increase topic retention
Whether partition 2's CURRENT-OFFSET is moving. If it is frozen, billing-3 is stuck (often on a poison message or a hung call); if it moves slowly, partition 2 has a hot key or billing-3 is slow
qs.e: Lag on one partition only points to that partition or its consumer, not to the cluster. Run the command twice a minute apart: a frozen offset and a slow-moving one need different fixes. Adding partitions also remaps keys.

qs.s: A new service reads the compacted topic below from the earliest offset. What does it receive?

code.title: create topic
code.src:
kafka-topics.sh --create --topic user-profiles --partitions 6 \
  --replication-factor 3 --config cleanup.policy=compact

o: Every change ever made to every profile

At least the latest value for each key. Some older values may still be there, because compaction runs in the background, and deleted keys (tombstones) disappear after a while. The consumer must handle several values per key
Only the events of the last 7 days
Nothing: compacted topics cannot be read from the beginning
qs.e: Compaction keeps the last value per key, which makes a topic usable as a changelog or table snapshot. It does not promise exactly one value per key at any moment, and it is not a full history.

qs.s: An SNS topic fans out to three SQS queues: email, analytics and search. The search team needs to process faster and wants 20 workers. What do they do?
o: Run 20 workers on the search SQS queue; they compete for its messages. Nothing changes for SNS or the other teams
Create 20 new SNS subscriptions
Ask the producer to publish each event 20 times
Move search to the email queue
qs.e: Fan-out (one copy per subscriber) and competing consumers (one copy shared by workers) work together: pub/sub between teams, a queue inside each team. More subscriptions would give each worker every message, so work would be done 20 times.

qs.s: A team enabled Kafka transactions and isolation.level=read_committed for “exactly-once”. Customers still sometimes get two emails after a consumer restart. Why?
o: Transactions are broken in Kafka
read_committed must be set on the producer

Kafka's exactly-once covers reading from Kafka and writing to Kafka atomically. Sending an email is outside Kafka, so a crash after sending but before the offset commit still repeats it. The email step needs its own idempotency
They need more partitions
qs.e: Exactly-once semantics in Kafka is real but limited to Kafka's own logs and offsets. Any external side effect (email, HTTP call, another database) must be made idempotent separately.

interview.q: What is the difference between a message queue and a pub/sub log like Kafka? How do you choose?
answer: Queue: each message is processed by one consumer and then deleted; good for distributing tasks (RabbitMQ, SQS).
Log: events are kept for a retention period; each consumer group reads independently at its own offset and can replay; ordering is per partition (Kafka, Redpanda, Kinesis).
Choose a queue for jobs, per-message retries, delays and DLQs; choose a log for many independent consumers, replay, stream processing and high throughput.
Logs need partition planning (key, count) and lag monitoring; queues need visibility timeouts and DLQ handling.
Managed or simpler options (SNS+SQS, Google Pub/Sub, NATS, Redis Streams) often fit before running Kafka yourself.
followups: How do you retry a single failed message in Kafka without blocking the partition?
What does replay give you in practice?

interview.q: How do you choose the partition key and partition count for a Kafka topic?
answer: Key = the entity whose events must stay in order (order ID, account ID); events of one key go to one partition.
Check skew: a key with a big share of traffic (one huge tenant) makes a hot partition; use a finer key or split known hot keys.
Partition count = the maximum consumer parallelism you will need in a group, with headroom, because adding partitions later remaps keys.
Too many partitions cost broker memory, file handles and slower rebalances; size from target throughput per partition.
Without a key, records are spread for balance but with no per-entity order.
followups: What happens to ordering when you add partitions?
How do you detect a hot partition?

interview.q: System design: design a pipeline that ingests click events from a website (about 1 million per minute) for real-time dashboards and daily reports.
answer: About 17,000 events/s: an edge collector batches events and writes to a Kafka-style log, keyed for even spread (for example session ID).
Stream processors (Flink, Kafka Streams, or simple consumers) aggregate per minute into a real-time store for dashboards.
A separate consumer group writes raw events to object storage in columnar files (Parquet) for daily batch reports and reprocessing.
Handle duplicates and late events: event IDs, event-time windows with a lateness allowance.
Size retention for replay after bugs, alert on consumer lag in seconds, and sample or drop at the collector under overload.
followups: How do you handle events that arrive an hour late?
How do you rebuild yesterday's numbers after a bug?

one: Services communicate by announcing facts that happened ("OrderPlaced") rather than calling each other with commands.
an: Posting a notice on the office board versus walking to each person's desk to tell them. The poster does not need to know who reads it.
how: Events are past-tense facts; commands are requests to do something. Choreography: services react to events with no central coordinator. Orchestration: a coordinator tells services what to do.
Event notification (thin: "order 42 changed", fetch details) vs event-carried state transfer (fat: includes the data).
Pairs naturally with the outbox pattern, sagas and CQRS.
why: Loose coupling between teams and services, natural audit trails, and easy extension.
trade: Flows become implicit and hard to trace ("why did this email go out?"). Eventual consistency everywhere. Needs tracing, schema registries and good event naming.

myth.r: It removes coupling at the cost of visibility. For simple request-response needs, a direct call is clearer.

o: SendWelcomeEmail
UserRegistered
DoBilling
UpdateStuff
q.e: Events describe what happened. Consumers decide what to do about it (send email, create trial, etc.).

more: Event notification vs event-carried state transfer vs event sourcing
lab: Add an in-process event bus to a small app: OrderPlaced triggers "send email" and "update stats" handlers. Then move one handler behind a real queue and compare.
docs: Martin Fowler: What do you mean by "Event-Driven"?

plain:
In an event-driven design, services announce facts that happened (“UserRegistered”, “PaymentFailed”) and other services decide for themselves how to react. Nobody calls the others directly to tell them what to do.

This keeps services loosely connected, but makes it harder to see the full flow of what happens after an action.
bridge: It is like a Redux action: you dispatch “USER_LOGGED_IN”, and several reducers and listeners react independently. The dispatcher does not call them one by one.

walk.title: Commands vs events for a new signup
steps: Command style: the signup service calls email.sendWelcome(), then billing.createTrial(), then analytics.track(). It knows about all three.
If the email service is down, signup fails or needs special handling.
Event style: signup saves the user and publishes UserRegistered. Done.
Email, billing and analytics each subscribe and react. If email is down, its messages wait; signup is unaffected.
The cost: to answer “what happens after signup?”, you need documentation or tracing, because no single file shows it.

terms: A fact in the past tense: something that happened.
Services react to events with no central controller.
A coordinator tells services what to do and in what order.
insights: Name events in the past tense (OrderShipped), not as instructions (SendEmail).
Treat each event type like a public API: an owner, a schema, a version, a list of consumers.
Alert on business output (invoices per hour), because a broken consumer often fails silently.

prod.summary: In production, event-driven systems fail quietly: an event goes out with the wrong schema, a consumer is down for hours, or nobody can explain why an email was sent. Seniors treat events as public APIs (versioned schemas, an owner, a catalog), make every consumer idempotent and observable, and keep trace context flowing through the broker.
checklist: Every event has an envelope: unique id, type, source, time and schema version (CloudEvents is a common standard for this).
Schema compatibility is checked in CI (schema registry or contract tests); only additive changes are allowed without a new version.
Events are published through an outbox or CDC, never with “save, then publish” as two separate steps.
Consumers are idempotent: they record processed event IDs or use upserts.
Trace context (traceparent) travels in message headers, so one trace shows the request and every async reaction.
Per-consumer lag and dead-letter counts are on a dashboard, with alerts and an owning team.
Each event type has an owner and a list of known consumers (an event catalog, for example AsyncAPI documents).
numbers: CloudEvents 1.0 required attributes: id, source, specversion, type. source + id must be unique, which gives consumers a ready-made dedup key.
W3C Trace Context: traceparent looks like 00-<32 hex trace-id>-<16 hex parent-id>-01 (55 characters).
Kafka keeps events for 7 days by default (log.retention.hours=168): a consumer that is down longer than that loses events unless retention is raised.
failures: Customers receive the welcome email twice after a broker failover.

At-least-once delivery redelivered the event and the email consumer is not idempotent. Record processed event IDs under a unique constraint and skip duplicates; also pass an idempotency key to the email provider if it supports one.
Billing stopped creating invoices three days ago, with no errors anywhere.

A producer renamed a field; the consumer read undefined and skipped the event. Validate schemas when publishing, check compatibility in CI, and alert on business output (invoices per hour), not only on errors.
Support asks “why did this user get a refund?” and it takes a day to answer.
Choreography without tracing. Propagate traceparent plus a correlation ID and the causing event ID in every event, and log them in every consumer.
Orders ship before they are paid: the shipping consumer handled OrderPlaced from one topic before PaymentCaptured arrived on another.
Ordering was assumed across different topics or keys. Key all events of one order to the same partition, or make consumers check state (“is it paid?”) instead of trusting arrival order.

code.title: CloudEvents-style envelope and an idempotent consumer
code.note: The dedup insert and the side effect share one transaction. For side effects outside your database (emails, payments), pass the event ID as the provider's idempotency key instead.

qs.s: OrderPlaced carries only { orderId }. Five consumers each call the orders API to fetch details. During a sale, the orders API falls over. Which change helps most?
o: Add more consumer instances
Remove caching from the orders API
Put the data consumers need into the event (event-carried state transfer), so they do not call back
Switch from events to direct commands
qs.e: Thin events create a “callback storm”: every event becomes N extra API calls to the producer. Fat events cost bigger messages and a stricter schema, but remove that load and that coupling.

qs.s: A teammate wants to rename the field total to totalCents in OrderPlaced. Six teams consume it. Safest plan?
o: Add totalCents next to total, move consumers over, and remove total later (or publish OrderPlaced.v2 in parallel)
Rename it and announce it in Slack
Rename it at night when traffic is low
Ask all six teams to deploy at the same time as the producer
qs.e: Events are a public contract with consumers you may not even know. Expand, migrate, then contract. A coordinated deploy of seven services is exactly the coupling events were supposed to remove.

qs.s: Which flow is a poor fit for pure choreography (only events, no coordinator)?
o: Sending a welcome email after signup
Updating the search index after a product changes
Recording analytics for each page view
A 6-step loan approval with deadlines, compensations and a status page for support
qs.e: Long flows with ordering, timeouts and undo steps become invisible when spread over many event handlers. An orchestrator or workflow engine keeps the flow in one place with visible state.

qs.s: This consumer keeps a read model of order status. The broker delivers at least once. Events: PAID (version 3), then SHIPPED (version 4), then a redelivery of PAID. What is the final status, and what is the fix?

code.title: order-view.ts

o: PAID: the redelivered old event overwrote the newer state. Store the version and update only if the event is newer: … SET status = $1, version = $3 WHERE id = $2 AND version < $3
SHIPPED, because brokers never redeliver old events
SHIPPED, because Postgres ignores repeated updates
The update fails with a conflict error
qs.e: Redelivery and reordering are normal in event-driven systems. A version guard makes the handler idempotent and order-safe at the same time. The tempting answer assumes the broker gives exactly-once, in-order delivery.

qs.s: This event goes to a Kafka topic kept forever so new services can replay history. A user asks you to delete their personal data. What is the problem, and what is a good design?

code.title: user.updated event

o: No problem: delete the user row in the users database
Delete the Kafka topic and recreate it
Ask every consumer team to remember to delete it

Personal data in a permanent log cannot be removed easily. Keep it out of long-lived events (send IDs; consumers that need contact data ask the owner service), or encrypt it with a per-user key and delete the key (crypto-shredding)
qs.e: Event logs and every consumer's copy are hard to clean. Designing events with minimal personal data is much cheaper than finding all copies later. Deleting the topic destroys everyone else's history.

qs.s: After a deploy, the broker shows millions of OrderUpdated events per minute, though users changed only a few orders. What is the most likely cause?
o: A broker bug that duplicates messages
Too few partitions

A handler consumes OrderUpdated, changes the order (for example sets updatedAt), and publishes OrderUpdated again: an event loop. Emit events only on real state changes, use specific event types, and carry a causation ID to detect cycles
Users refreshing their pages
qs.e: Choreography can create cycles that no single file shows. Specific events (OrderShipped, not OrderUpdated) and causation IDs make loops visible and easy to stop.

qs.s: The order flow cannot continue until billing has created an invoice and returned its number. Should the order service publish an InvoiceNeeded event and hope billing reacts?
o: Yes: everything should be an event
No: this is a command with one specific receiver and a needed result. Use a direct call or a command message with a reply, owned by an orchestrator, and publish events about the facts afterwards
Yes, and poll the billing database for the invoice
No: use a shared database table instead
qs.e: Events announce facts to whoever cares. When the sender needs a specific action and its outcome, that is a command. Disguising commands as events hides the dependency instead of removing it.

interview.q: What is the difference between events and commands, and between choreography and orchestration?
answer: Event: a past-tense fact (“OrderPlaced”); the producer does not know or care who reacts. Command: a request to a specific receiver (“CreateInvoice”) that can be rejected.
Choreography: services react to each other's events with no central controller; loose coupling, but the flow is implicit.
Orchestration: a coordinator (often a workflow engine) tells services what to do and tracks state; the flow is visible in one place.
Use choreography for simple reactions with independent consumers (emails, indexing, analytics); use orchestration for multi-step business flows with deadlines and compensations.
Many systems combine both: an orchestrator inside one flow, events between bounded contexts.
followups: How do you see the whole flow in a choreographed system?
Thin events or fat events?

interview.q: System design: design order processing (orders, payments, inventory, shipping) with events. How do you keep it reliable and observable?
answer: Each service owns its data and publishes events through an outbox, so no event is lost and none is sent for a rolled-back change.
Events are keyed by order ID for per-order ordering; consumers are idempotent and check state instead of trusting arrival order.
The multi-step part (reserve, pay, ship, compensate) is an orchestrated saga; other reactions (emails, analytics) subscribe freely.
Observability: trace context in message headers, correlation and causation IDs, per-consumer lag and DLQ alerts, an event catalog with owners.
Business metrics as alerts (orders paid but not shipped after N hours), because silent consumer failures produce no errors.
followups: What happens when the shipping consumer is down for a day?
How do you replay events safely?

interview.q: How do you evolve event schemas without breaking consumers?
answer: Treat events as public APIs: registered schemas (Avro, Protobuf or JSON Schema) and compatibility checks in CI before the producer deploys.
Additive changes only within a version: new optional fields; consumers ignore unknown fields.
Breaking changes: expand and contract (add the new field, migrate consumers, remove later) or publish a new event version in parallel.
Know your consumers: an event catalog and owner per event type.
For stored events (event sourcing, long retention), keep old versions readable with upcasters forever.
followups: What is backward vs forward compatibility in a schema registry?
How long do you keep publishing the old version?
