one: Quick order-of-magnitude math on traffic, storage and bandwidth to check whether a design is plausible.
an: Before planning a party, you estimate guests × slices to know whether you need 3 pizzas or 30, without counting crumbs.
how: 1 day ≈ 86,400 s ≈ 10<sup>5</sup> s. So 1M requests/day ≈ 12 requests/second average; peak is often 2–10× that.
Latencies to remember: memory ~100ns, SSD read ~100µs, same-datacentre round trip ~0.5ms, cross-continent ~100–150ms.
Storage: 10M users × 1KB profile = 10GB (fits in RAM). 1M photos/day × 2MB = 2TB/day (object storage, CDN, lifecycle rules).
why: It is how you decide whether you need a cache, a queue, sharding, or nothing at all. It is also expected in every system-design interview.
trade: Being right within 10× is the goal. Precision is wasted effort; stating assumptions clearly is not.

myth.m: Our app with 100k users needs a distributed architecture.
myth.r: Do the math. 100k users might be 5 requests per second, which a single small server handles easily.

q.s: An app expects 50M page views per month, each making 3 API calls. Average API requests per second?
o: About 6
About 58
About 5,800
About 580,000
q.e: 150M / (30 × 86,400 ≈ 2.6M s) ≈ 58/s average. Plan for a few hundred at peak.

plain:
Back-of-the-envelope estimation is quick rough math to check whether a design makes sense: how many requests per second, how much storage per year, how much bandwidth. Being right within a factor of 10 is enough.

It stops you from building a complicated system for tiny traffic, or a tiny system for huge traffic.
bridge: You already do this for bundles: “300KB on a 1.6 Mbps mobile connection is about 1.5 seconds.” The same habit applies to servers and databases.

walk.title: Does a chat app with 100,000 daily users need sharding?
steps: Assume each user sends 20 messages a day: 2 million messages/day.
A day has about 86,400 seconds (≈ 100,000). Average ≈ 20 messages/second; peak maybe 5× → 100/second.
Each message about 1KB with metadata → 2GB per day → about 730GB per year.
A single Postgres server handles thousands of simple writes per second; 730GB fits on one disk.
Conclusion: no sharding needed. Partition by month for easy cleanup. Revisit at 10× growth.

terms: How much higher the busiest time is than average.
Rough costs of operations: memory ~100ns, SSD ~100µs, cross-ocean ~150ms.
insights: State assumptions out loud; in reviews and interviews, the reasoning matters more than the number.
Estimate the resource that runs out first: connections, IOPS, egress or a partner's rate limit, not only CPU.
Compare the estimate with real metrics after launch, and fix the assumptions that were wrong.

prod.summary: Seniors use estimation in design reviews and capacity planning, not only interviews. Before adding a queue, a cache or a shard, they compute peak requests per second, data growth, connection counts and cost, and compare them with what one machine can do. The numbers are rough; the habit of checking prevents both over-engineering and outages.
checklist: Estimate the peak, not the average: use real traffic graphs when they exist (peak-to-average is often 2–10×), and add launch or campaign spikes.
Convert to the resource that runs out first: DB connections, IOPS, CPU per request, memory, egress, or a partner's rate limit.
Storage includes indexes, replicas, backups and retention: data × copies × (1 + index overhead) × years.
Use Little's law for concurrency: in-flight requests = arrival rate × time in system (500 req/s × 0.2 s = 100).
Write assumptions in the design doc so others can challenge them, and compare them with production metrics after launch.
Estimate cost too: egress, per-request managed-service pricing and log volume often cost more than CPU.
numbers: 1 day ≈ 86,400 s ≈ 10<sup>5</sup> s; 1 million requests/day ≈ 12 req/s average; 1 TB/day of transfer ≈ 93 Mbit/s average.
Classic latency numbers (Jeff Dean, Peter Norvig): main memory reference ~100 ns, round trip in one datacentre ~0.5 ms, California–Netherlands round trip ~150 ms.
PostgreSQL default max_connections is 100, and each connection is a separate process: 20 app pods × a pool of 10 already needs 200.
Little's law: L = λ × W. At 300 req/s with 50 ms of DB time each, about 15 queries are in flight on average.
failures: After autoscaling from 10 to 40 pods, the database rejects connections: FATAL: sorry, too many clients already.
Nobody multiplied pods × pool size: 40 × 10 = 400 > 100. Put PgBouncer (transaction pooling) in front, and size pools from the database limit down.
The cloud bill is 5× the estimate; the biggest line is data transfer.
The estimate counted storage and CPU but not egress (images served straight from object storage). Put a CDN in front, resize images, and estimate bytes per page view × views.
A disk-full alert fires 8 months after launch.
The storage estimate ignored indexes, WAL and backups, and assumed no growth. Track real GB per day, project it, and alert at 70–80% with “days until full”.
A small new feature hits a partner API limit of 10 req/s on its first day.
Fan-out at peak was not estimated: 1 user action = 5 partner calls, × 200 actions/s. Batch, cache or queue the calls under the partner's limit.

code.title: A written estimate for a design doc
code.note: The decision at the end is the point. Write the assumptions so a reviewer can say “uploads per user is 5, not 0.5” and the numbers update.
code.src:
Feature: photo uploads for a marketplace
Assumptions (write them down so others can challenge them)
  daily active users     = 200,000
  uploads per user/day   = 0.5     -> 100,000 uploads/day
  stored per upload      = 400 KB photo + 3 thumbnails (~60 KB) = 460 KB
  peak-to-average        = 5x

Traffic
  100,000 / 86,400       ~ 1.2 uploads/s average  ->  ~6/s at peak
Storage
  100,000 x 460 KB       ~ 46 GB/day  ->  ~17 TB/year (object storage handles replicas)
Egress (the real cost)
  200,000 users x 50 photo views x 100 KB = 1 TB/day  ~ 93 Mbit/s average

Decision
  6 uploads/s: one API service is enough; no queue needed for ingest.
  Put a CDN in front and serve small WebP/AVIF thumbnails.
  Revisit if daily active users grow 10x.

qs.s: An API handles 400 req/s at peak, and each request holds a database connection for 25 ms. How many connections are busy on average?
qs.e: Little's law: 400 × 0.025 s = 10 connections in use on average. Add headroom for bursts and slow queries (for example a pool of 20–30), not 400.

qs.s: A chat app has 2 million daily users. Each sends 40 messages per day; each message takes about 300 bytes stored, with indexes. Storage per year, one copy?
o: About 900 GB
About 9 TB
About 90 TB
About 24 GB
qs.e: 2M × 40 = 80M messages/day × 300 B = 24 GB/day × 365 ≈ 8.8 TB/year. 24 GB is one day; replicas and backups multiply the yearly figure.

qs.s: Product says “we will have 1 million users”. Which follow-up question changes the design the most?
o: Which cloud region we deploy to
Which programming language the backend uses
How many are active at the same time, and how many requests and writes each makes per minute at peak
How many engineers will work on it
qs.e: Registered users say little. Peak concurrent users × actions per user gives requests and writes per second, which decide caching, queues and database size.

qs.s: Find the mistake in this estimate from a design doc.

code.title: estimate.txt
code.src:
daily active users  = 10,000,000
reads per user/day  = 50
read QPS (average)  = 10,000,000 x 50 / 86,400 = 5,787,037 /s
=> we need about 6,000 cache servers at 1,000 QPS each

o: Reads per user should be 500
A day has 3,600 seconds
500 million ÷ 86,400 is about 5,800 per second, not 5.8 million. The error is 1,000×, and it turns a few servers into thousands. Peak is maybe 3–5× higher, about 20,000–30,000 QPS
Cache servers handle only 100 QPS
qs.e: Do a sanity check with powers of ten: 5 × 10<sup>8</sup> ÷ 10<sup>5</sup> ≈ 5 × 10<sup>3</sup>. Also, one Redis node serves far more than 1,000 QPS, so the conclusion was wrong twice.

qs.s: A live stream has 200,000 concurrent viewers at 3 Mbit/s each. What egress do you need, and what follows?

code.title: assumptions
code.src:
concurrent viewers  = 200,000
bitrate per viewer  = 3 Mbit/s
origin server NIC   = 25 Gbit/s

o: 600 Gbit/s (75 GB/s): far beyond a few origin servers, so a CDN must serve the viewers and the origin serves only the CDN
600 Mbit/s: one server is enough
6 Tbit/s: impossible to serve
60 Gbit/s: three origin servers are enough
qs.e: 200,000 × 3 Mbit/s = 600,000 Mbit/s = 600 Gbit/s. Bits versus bytes and Mbit versus Gbit are the classic slips; divide by 8 for bytes.

qs.s: A social app has 100 million daily users. Each posts 2 times a day and has 200 followers on average. With fan-out on write (copy each post into every follower's timeline), how many timeline inserts per second is that on average?
o: About 2,300 per second
About 46,000 per second
About 4.6 million per second
About 460,000 per second
qs.e: 2 × 10<sup>8</sup> posts/day ÷ 86,400 ≈ 2,300 posts/s; × 200 followers ≈ 463,000 inserts/s, before peaks. This is why big systems mix fan-out on write for normal users with fan-out on read for accounts with millions of followers.

qs.s: 50 million registered users, each session record about 2 KB. About 5 million users are active on a busy day. Can sessions live in one Redis node with 64 GB of memory?
o: No: 50M × 2 KB = 100 GB, so you need a cluster no matter what
Yes, if only active sessions are stored with a TTL: 5M × 2 KB ≈ 10 GB, plus Redis overhead per key, well under 64 GB. Use a replica for availability
Yes, Redis compresses all values automatically
No: Redis cannot store more than 1 million keys
qs.e: Size the working set, not the total user count. Sessions expire, so only active ones take memory. Keep headroom for per-key overhead and growth, and still plan for failover.

interview.q: System design: estimate the QPS and storage for a URL shortener that creates 100 million new short URLs per month.
answer: Writes: 10<sup>8</sup> ÷ (30 × 86,400 ≈ 2.6 × 10<sup>6</sup> s) ≈ 40 writes/s average; maybe 200/s at peak.
Reads: assume 100 reads per URL over its life, so roughly 100× writes: about 4,000 reads/s average, more at peak; cache hot URLs.
Storage: about 500 bytes per record (long URL, code, metadata) × 1.2 × 10<sup>9</sup> per year ≈ 600 GB/year before indexes and replicas.
Key space: 7 base-62 characters give 62<sup>7</sup> ≈ 3.5 × 10<sup>12</sup> codes, enough for centuries at this rate.
Conclusion: one relational database plus a cache can handle years of this; state the assumptions so they can be challenged.
followups: How do you generate short codes without collisions?
What changes if reads are 10× higher?

interview.q: Walk me through how you would estimate how many servers a new service needs.
answer: Peak requests per second from users × actions per user × peak-to-average ratio (use real traffic graphs if they exist).
Cost per request from a benchmark or a similar service (CPU ms, memory, DB queries), then requests per second per instance at a safe utilisation (for example 60%).
Use Little's law for concurrency: in-flight = rate × latency; check connection pools and database limits.
Add headroom for losing a zone (N+1 or N+2) and for deploys.
Validate with a load test and compare with production metrics after launch.
followups: Which resource usually runs out first?
How do you estimate cost per request?

interview.q: Estimate the monthly cost drivers of serving images for an Instagram-like app with 10 million daily users.
answer: Views: say 100 images per user per day = 10<sup>9</sup> image views/day.
Bytes: about 100 KB per optimised image = 100 TB/day of egress, about 3 PB/month; that dominates the bill.
Therefore: a CDN with a high cache hit rate, modern formats (WebP/AVIF), several sizes per image, and negotiated bandwidth pricing.
Storage: uploads (for example 10<sup>7</sup>/day × 2 MB original + sizes) grow by petabytes per year; lifecycle rules move old originals to cheaper tiers.
Compute for resizing is small next to egress; estimate it last.
followups: How would the numbers change with video?
How do you measure the CDN hit rate's effect on cost?

one: Engines (Temporal, AWS Step Functions, Inngest, Vercel Workflow) that run multi-step processes reliably, persisting progress so they survive crashes and can wait for days.
an: A recipe card that ticks off each step as you finish it. If you are called away mid-cooking, anyone can pick up exactly where you left off.
how: You write the process as code or a state machine: charge → wait for shipment webhook (up to 7 days) → send review request after 14 days.
The engine records each step's result. After a crash it replays from history and continues; retries and timeouts are built in.
Replaces fragile combos of cron jobs, status columns and queue chains.
why: Onboarding sequences, payment flows, sagas and AI agent loops are all long-running processes that ad-hoc code handles badly.
trade: Another system to learn and run. Workflow code has rules (determinism) that surprise newcomers.

myth.m: A cron job checking a status column every minute is a workflow engine.
myth.r: It is the start of one, without history, retries, visibility or correctness under concurrency.

q.s: A subscription flow: trial → reminder day 12 → charge day 14 → retry failed charges 3 times over a week. Best fit?
o: setTimeout
A durable workflow engine (or a well-designed job scheduler)
A CDN
A bigger database
q.e: Long waits, retries and state that must survive deploys are exactly what workflow engines provide.

more: Deterministic workflow code and why it matters for replay
Alternatives: Inngest, Trigger.dev, Step Functions, Vercel Workflow
lab: Run Temporal's TypeScript hello-world sample locally. Add a 30-second sleep step, kill the worker during the sleep, restart it, and watch the workflow continue.

plain: Some processes take hours or days and have many steps: start a trial, remind on day 12, charge on day 14, retry failed charges. A durable workflow engine runs this kind of process reliably. It saves progress after each step, so if a server restarts, the workflow continues where it stopped.
bridge: Without an engine, this logic gets spread across cron jobs, status columns and queue handlers, and nobody can see where a given customer is in the flow. The engine makes it one readable function.

walk.title: A subscription trial as one workflow
steps: Code reads top to bottom: createTrial(); await sleep('12 days'); sendReminder(); await sleep('2 days'); charge();.
The engine records each finished step. During the 12-day sleep, nothing runs and nothing is held in memory.
On day 9 you deploy a new version and all workers restart. The workflow is unaffected; the timer is stored in the engine and fires on day 12.

The charge fails because the payment provider returns 503. The engine retries the charge activity after 1 minute, then 2, then 4 (up to 5 attempts). A declined card is a business error and is not retried.
Support looks up a customer and sees exactly which step their workflow is on and its history.

terms: Progress is saved so the process survives crashes and restarts.
One unit of work with side effects, like charging a card.
Workflow code must behave the same when replayed from history.
insights: Side effects belong in activities or steps with stable idempotency keys, never in workflow code.
Changing workflow code while executions are running needs versioning and replay tests in CI.
Long loops need continue-as-new, or history hits the engine's size limit.

prod.summary: In production, durable workflow engines (Temporal, AWS Step Functions, Inngest, Vercel Workflow) replace cron jobs plus status columns for long multi-step processes. Seniors watch the engine's rules: workflow code must be deterministic, side effects go into idempotent activities or steps, history size is limited, and changing code for running workflows needs versioning.
checklist: Side effects (HTTP, database, email, payments) happen only in activities or steps, each idempotent with a stable key, never directly in workflow code.
Activities have timeouts (Temporal: startToCloseTimeout) and an explicit retry policy with a max attempts or expiration; business errors are non-retryable.
Long-running or looping workflows use continue-as-new (Temporal) or child workflows, so history stays small.
New workflow code is safe for executions already running (Temporal patching or worker versioning; Step Functions versions and aliases), and replay tests run in CI.
Payloads are small: large data goes to object storage and the workflow passes a reference.
Dashboards show running, failed and timed-out executions; failed ones have a retry or redrive procedure.
Workflow IDs are business IDs (trial-user-42), so starting the same workflow twice is rejected instead of duplicated.
numbers: Temporal: event history is limited to 51,200 events or 50 MB per execution; warnings start at 10,240 events or 10 MB.
Temporal activity retry defaults: initial interval 1 s, backoff coefficient 2, max interval 100 s, unlimited attempts. Workflows themselves do not retry by default.
AWS Step Functions: Standard runs up to 1 year with at most 25,000 history events; Express runs up to 5 minutes; input or output per state is limited to 256 KiB.
failures: After a deploy, Temporal workflow tasks fail with a DeterminismViolationError / nondeterminism error.

Workflow code changed (a step was added or reordered) while executions were running, so replay no longer matches history. Use patched() or worker versioning, and run replay tests against saved histories in CI.
A workflow that polls a partner every hour fails after some months with a history size error.
Each loop adds events until the 51,200-event limit. Call continue-as-new every N iterations (Temporal also sets workflowInfo().continueAsNewSuggested).
A customer was charged twice; history shows the charge activity was retried after a timeout.
The provider processed the charge but the activity timed out before reporting success, so it was retried. Pass an idempotency key built from the workflow ID and step name.
A Step Functions execution fails with States.DataLimitExceeded.
A state's output was larger than 256 KiB. Store the data in S3 and pass the object key between states.

code.title: Temporal (TypeScript): a 14-day trial as one durable function
code.note: All I/O happens in activities, which Temporal records and retries. The charge gets a stable idempotency key, because an activity can be retried after it already succeeded at the provider. The activity must throw ApplicationFailure.create({ type: "CardDeclined" }) (or an Error subclass named CardDeclined). Setting err.name on a plain Error is not enough: the type stays Error and the decline is retried 5 times.

qs.s: Inside a Temporal workflow function, a developer writes const res = await fetch(pricingUrl). What is the problem?
o: Nothing: Temporal records the response automatically
fetch is just slower inside workflows
Workflow code is replayed and must be deterministic; network I/O belongs in an activity, which Temporal records and retries
It only works with axios, not fetch
qs.e: On replay the workflow function runs again; a live network call could return something different and break the replay. Activities run once per attempt, and their results are stored in history.

qs.s: A Temporal workflow loops forever: every hour it calls an activity to check a partner API. After some months it fails. Why, and what is the fix?
o: History grows with every iteration until it hits the 51,200-event limit; use continue-as-new periodically
Timers expire after one year
The worker leaks memory
Activities can only be called 10,000 times
qs.e: Every timer and activity adds several events to history. Continue-as-new starts a fresh execution with the same workflow ID and a small history, carrying over only the state you pass.

qs.s: Which job is NOT worth a durable workflow engine?
o: Onboarding: wait up to 7 days for a KYC webhook, then provision the account
Resizing an uploaded image in under 2 s, safe to redo if it fails
A refund flow across the payment provider, inventory and email
Monthly invoicing with retries spread over several days
qs.e: A short, idempotent task is a plain background job: if it fails, run it again. Engines pay off when there are long waits, several side effects, compensation or a need to see progress.

qs.s: 40,000 trial workflows are currently sleeping for 12 days. You deploy this change. What happens when they wake up?

code.title: workflows.ts (Temporal)

o: They all send the welcome email and continue normally

Replay no longer matches their history (history has the timer where the new code schedules an activity), so their workflow tasks fail with a nondeterminism error and they stop progressing. Guard the change: if (patched('welcome-email')) await sendWelcomeEmail(userId);
Temporal skips the new line for old workflows automatically
They restart from the beginning
qs.e: Running workflows replay their history against the new code, step by step. Adding or reordering commands breaks that match. Patching (or worker versioning) lets old executions keep the old path while new ones take the new path.

qs.s: The worker pod running exportReport is killed 1 minute into the activity. When will Temporal retry it?

code.title: workflows.ts

o: Immediately, because Temporal sees the pod die
Never; activities are not retried after a crash
After 1 minute

Only when the 10-minute startToCloseTimeout expires, because the server cannot tell a dead worker from a slow one. For long activities, send heartbeats and set a short heartbeatTimeout so failures are noticed in seconds
qs.e: The server only learns about a lost activity from a timeout. Heartbeats give it a fast signal and can also carry progress, so the retry can continue where the last attempt stopped.

qs.s: You need: “3 days after signup, send a reminder unless the user has verified their email.” You do not run a workflow engine. What is the simplest robust design?
o: Enqueue a delayed job (run at signup + 3 days) whose handler checks the user's current state and sends only if still unverified; make it idempotent
A setTimeout for 3 days in the API process
A cron job every minute that scans all users and keeps state in memory
Send the reminder immediately and ignore verification
qs.e: One wait and one check is a delayed job, not a workflow. Checking current state at run time handles verification that happened in between. In-process timers die with the pod.

qs.s: A loan workflow must wait up to 5 days for a manager's approval, then escalate. How do you model the wait in a durable workflow engine such as Temporal?
o: Poll the database every second from inside the workflow
Have the manager's UI call the workflow's activity directly
Deliver the approval as a signal (or update) to the workflow and wait with a timeout, for example await condition(() => approved, '5 days'); if it returns false, run the escalation
Start a new workflow every day
qs.e: Signals bring outside events into a running workflow, and durable timers make long waits free. Polling from workflow code wastes history events and resources.

interview.q: What is durable execution, and how does an engine like Temporal survive crashes?
answer: The engine stores an event history for every workflow: activities scheduled and completed, timers, signals.
Workflow code is deterministic orchestration; after a crash any worker replays the history through the code to rebuild state, then continues.
Side effects run in activities, which have timeouts and retry policies; their results are stored, so they are not repeated on replay.
Timers are stored on the server, so a workflow can sleep for days with nothing in memory.
Rules that follow: no I/O or randomness in workflow code (use the SDK's versions), version code changes, keep histories bounded (continue-as-new).

interview.q: System design: design subscription billing with trials, renewals, failed-payment retries and dunning emails.
answer: One long-running workflow (or a state machine) per subscription with a business ID, so it cannot start twice.
Timers for trial end and each renewal; charging in an activity with an idempotency key such as subscriptionId:period.
Failed payments: a retry schedule over days (for example day 1, 3, 7) with dunning emails between them, then suspend; card updates arrive as signals and trigger an immediate retry.
Plan changes, cancellations and refunds as signals or updates; the ledger records every money movement.
Long-lived workflows use continue-as-new each period; dashboards show subscriptions stuck in dunning.
followups: How do you handle a price change for 1 million running subscriptions?
What if the payment provider is down for a day?

interview.q: When would you NOT use a workflow engine? What does it cost?
answer: Short, idempotent background jobs (resize an image, send one email) are simpler on a job queue.
The engine is another critical system to run or pay for (a database, workers, upgrades) and to monitor.
Developers must learn determinism rules, versioning and replay testing; mistakes show up as stuck workflows after deploys.
Payload and history limits push large data to object storage.
Use it when there are long waits, several side effects, compensations, human steps or a need to see each process's state.

diagrams.caption: What to notice: no worker waits 14 days. The engine stores the history and the timers; after a restart a worker replays the history and continues. The same idempotency key on the retry prevents a double charge.
